papers.title: Assessment of bowel preparation quality in dogs undergoing colonoscopy using the Boston Bowel Preparation Scale.
papers.authors: Ruedi GL, Kook PH
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of a bowel preparation protocol consisting of at-home administration of clear broth and polyethylene glycol 3350 followed by colonic flushing immediately before colonoscopy in dogs. METHODS: In this single-referral-center retrospective study, dogs with complete video documentation of the colon were included. Colonic cleanliness was assessed using the Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS), which scores the 3 colonic segments individually (total score range, 0 to 9 with higher scores indicating better preparation quality). Adequate preparation was defined as a total BBPS score ≥ 6 with no individual segment score < 2. RESULTS: Video footage from 49 colonoscopies performed in 47 dogs was assessed by a single examiner. Adequate colonic preparation was achieved in 41 of 49 (84%) colonoscopies. Median total BBPS score was 7 (range, 4 to 9), with median segment scores of 3, 2, and 2 for descending, transverse, and ascending colon, respectively. The ascending colon had significantly lower scores than the descending colon. In 57% of procedures, the indication for colonoscopy was evaluation of chronic enteropathy (combined upper and lower intestinal endoscopy) without specific suspicion of colonic disease. CONCLUSIONS: High-quality bowel preparation for colonoscopy can be achieved without complex or logistically demanding protocols. A straightforward, owner-friendly, at-home preparation regimen provided diagnostic-quality colonic visualization in dogs. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings may facilitate broader clinical use of colonoscopy in dogs by supporting practical bowel preparation protocols that are feasible for owners and sufficient for diagnostic evaluation, particularly when complete colonic cleanliness is not essential for the intended diagnostic objective.

papers.title: Surgical management of cricopharyngeal achalasia in dogs results in low mortality but moderate incidence of recurrence or persistent clinical signs.
papers.authors: Zhang RM, Brisson BA, Holt DE, Park B, Ham KM, Hawker W
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe diagnostic and surgical management of cricopharyngeal achalasia (CA) in dogs and to identify patient or management factors that may contribute to postoperative outcomes. METHODS: Signalment, diagnostic imaging findings, surgical information, complications, and outcomes were retrospectively obtained. Fisher exact and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were performed to identify predictors of unsatisfactory outcomes using sex, breed, age, videofluoroscopic swallow study findings, laterality of surgery, and muscles resected as variables. RESULTS: 26 dogs surgically managed for CA from 2009 through 2025 were included. The most common breeds were Poodle mixes (n = 12) and Golden Retrievers (8). Ventral bilateral surgery resulted in shorter operative times than through 2 lateral incisions. Postoperative complication and mortality rates were 23% and 11.5%, respectively. Aspiration pneumonia was the most common postoperative complication. Unsatisfactory outcomes were reported in 42.3%. Recurrence of clinical signs after initial resolution was noted in 34.6%, and revision surgery was performed in 26.9%. Median time to recurrence was 84 days (range, 7 to 1,320 days). No significant association was identified for age, sex, breed, laterality, videofluoroscopic swallow study findings, or muscles resected. CONCLUSIONS: Surgical management of CA resulted in low mortality, moderate incidence of recurrence and revision surgery, and residual symptoms requiring long-term conservative management. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Surgery is a safe option for management of CA, but owners should be informed of the risks of recurrence and residual clinical signs that may require long-term dietary modifications. Animals with CA are at risk of aspiration pneumonia both pre- and postoperatively and should be monitored accordingly.

papers.title: Cytokine priming shifts mitochondrial architecture and extracellular vesicle cargo of feline placental mesenchymal stromal cells toward an immunosuppressive phenotype.
papers.authors: Soltero-Rivera M, Arzi B, Marycz K
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To characterize effects of inflammatory cytokine priming on viability, mitochondrial morphology, and extracellular vesicle (EV) cargo in feline placenta-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs). METHODS: Feline placenta-derived MSCs from 7 healthy cats were cultured under control, serum-deprived, or cytokine-stimulated (tumor necrosis factor-α, interferon-γ, IL-1, IL-6) conditions in vitro. Viability/apoptosis were assessed by flow cytometry and mitochondrial morphology by confocal microscopy with MicroP/MATLAB; EVs were characterized by surface markers, RNA sequencing, and microRNA (miR) profiling. RESULTS: Viability exceeded 96% across all conditions, with no significant intergroup differences. Kiel 67 proliferation marker and metabolic activity were significantly reduced under serum-free and cytokine-stimulated conditions versus controls (both P < .001). Cytokine priming increased branching and simple tubular mitochondria, whereas serum deprivation increased fragmented forms. Extracellular vesicle transcriptomics identified 329 differentially expressed genes, including upregulated immunosuppressive receptors C-C motif chemokine receptor 8 and poliovirus receptor-related immunoglobulin domain-containing protein and downregulated proinflammatory histone transcripts. microRNA (miR) profiling revealed 23 differentially expressed miRs, with enrichment of anti-inflammatory miR-204, let-7g, and miR-181b-2 and depletion of proinflammatory miR-34a and miR-320a. CONCLUSIONS: Cytokine priming induces mitochondrial elongation and shifts EV cargo toward an immunosuppressive phenotype without compromising viability, supporting inflammatory priming as a strategy to optimize MSC-based therapies for T-cell-mediated inflammatory diseases. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Inflammatory priming prior to MSC administration may enhance therapeutic efficacy in cats, supporting investigation of cytokine licensing as a translatable approach to improving MSC therapy outcomes in veterinary medicine.

papers.title: Extended Reality for Image-Guided Small Animal Surgery: Current Evidence, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions.
papers.authors: Caivano D, Valeri F, Corda A, Bufalari A
papers.abstract: Image-guided surgery has become an integral component of modern veterinary surgery using advanced imaging modalities, such as computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasonography, and fluoroscopy. Recently, extended reality (XR) technologies have emerged as promising tools to enhance image-guided surgical procedures by improving three-dimensional anatomical understanding, surgical navigation, and intraoperative decision-making. Although XR has gained considerable attention in human surgery, its application in veterinary surgery remains at an early stage. This narrative review aimed to provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence regarding XR technologies in small animal surgery, with particular emphasis on their integration with preoperative and intraoperative imaging modalities. The available literature was reviewed to evaluate current clinical applications, technological developments and future perspectives. A literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published up to May 2026 using combinations of terms related to extended reality and small animal veterinary surgery. Original articles, case reports, pilot studies, technical reports, and reviews addressing clinical, experimental, or simulation-based applications were considered. Although several studies have explored the use of XR technologies for veterinary education, anatomical training, and diagnostic imaging instruction, relatively few investigations have assessed their direct application in clinical surgical practice. Potential applications have been described in orthopedic, oncologic, neurologic, cardiovascular, and minimally invasive procedures. Crucially, the currently available peer-reviewed evidence is restricted to canine patients, as no eligible feline studies were identified. Current evidence suggests that XR is an emerging technology with potential applications in canine surgical planning, image-guided procedures, and surgical training. Further prospective clinical studies are required to establish its clinical effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and impact on surgical outcomes.

papers.title: Perioperative analgesic effects of opiranserin in canine castration: a pilot study.
papers.authors: Lee S, Oh S, Lee I, Son WG
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Opiranserin, a non-opioid analgesic acting as a glycine transporter 2 inhibitor and 5-HT2A receptor antagonist, was evaluated for reducing intraoperative rescue analgesia and postoperative pain in dogs undergoing castration under isoflurane anesthesia. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eight healthy male Beagle dogs were randomized to receive a continuous rate infusion of opiranserin (5 mg·kg-1·h-1 for 1 h before induction, then 0.33 mg·kg-1·h-1 for 9 h; n = 4) or 0.9% saline (n = 4). Anesthesia was induced with alfaxalone and maintained with isoflurane (1.5% end-tidal); all dogs received meloxicam and cefazolin preoperatively, without locoregional analgesia. Hemodynamic responses (ΔMAP, ΔHR) were recorded across 11 surgical events; rescue remifentanil was given when both increased ≥20% from baseline. Postoperative pain was scored with the Glasgow Composite Measure Pain Scale-Short Form (GCMPS-SF) from 30 min after extubation (T0) through T7, with rescue analgesia at scores ≥5. Primary outcomes were intraoperative rescue analgesia frequency and postoperative GCMPS-SF scores; secondary outcomes were intraoperative hemodynamic responses, postoperative rescue consumption, and adverse effects. Data were analyzed with Mann-Whitney U tests and linear mixed models with Bonferroni-adjusted comparisons. RESULTS: The opiranserin group required fewer intraoperative rescue interventions than the normal saline group (median 2 [2-2] vs. 6.5 [3-9]; p = 0.021). GCMPS-SF scores showed significant effects of group (p = 0.030), time (p = 0.047), and group × time interaction (p = 0.034), with lower scores in the opiranserin group at T1 (adjusted p = 0.012) but not at other time points. Among secondary outcomes, significant overall effects of group were found for ΔMAP (p = 0.011) and ΔHR (p = 0.048), and of surgical event for both (p < 0.001 and p = 0.008), with no group × event interaction; no individual event differed significantly after correction. Cumulative postoperative rescue analgesic consumption and the incidence of adverse effects did not differ between groups. CONCLUSION: These preliminary findings suggest that opiranserin may reduce intraoperative rescue analgesia requirements and attenuate postoperative pain in dogs, warranting confirmation in larger trials. The absence of significant adverse effects is reassuring but should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size.

papers.title: Complete blood count interpretation in dogs and cats and its analytical compatibility with Vis-NIR point-of-care hematology: A systematic literature review with narrative synthesis.
papers.authors: Bisiaux T, da Costa JM, Martins RC, Barroso TG
papers.abstract: This systematic literature review with narrative synthesis assessed the diagnostic contribution of complete blood count (CBC) interpretation in dogs and cats combined only with anamnesis and physical examination, without biochemistry or imaging, and the compatibility of the CBC variables and CBC-derived indices identified with emerging point-of-care (POC) hematology platforms using visible-short-wave-near-infrared (Vis-NIR) spectroscopy and self-learning artificial intelligence (SLAI). Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, studies published from 2015 to January 2026 were identified and integrated into tables associating hematological patterns, CBC-derived indices, clinical presentation, and differential diagnoses. The technology component was appraised separately for analytical compatibility, not as an independent systematic review. Recurrent signatures included inflammatory leukograms, regenerative and non-regenerative anemia, stress leukograms, leukopenic syndromes, and thrombocytopenic disorders. Conventional CBC findings and CBC-derived indices (neutrophil-to-lymphocyte, monocyte-to-lymphocyte, platelet-to-neutrophil and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratios, and the systemic immune-inflammation index) were investigated across infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic, endocrine, cardiovascular, and immune-mediated diseases. However, this evidence is concentrated on pyometra, parvovirosis, pancreatitis, parasitism, cardiopathies and endocrinopathies, derives predominantly from small studies in dogs; these indices remain non-specific markers of systemic inflammatory burden. For POC technology, proof-of-concept studies report agreement with reference analyzers for erythrocyte parameters and total leukocyte counts, but not for the differential and platelet counts several of these indices require. Analytical compatibility is therefore supported for selected CBC parameters, but not clinical validity for CBC-derived indices or disease diagnosis. Whether these platforms can enable rapid, minimally invasive, decentralized CBC monitoring, particularly in fragile, pediatric, geriatric, chronic, and palliative-care patients, remains to be demonstrated in clinical studies.

papers.title: Cardiac Chemodectoma With Recurrent Pericardial Effusion and Cardiac Tamponade in an Alaskan Malamute: A Case Report.
papers.authors: Patil S, Mhase A, Rai S, Raut M, Sharma A
papers.abstract: Chemodectomas (aortic body tumors) are rare, slow-growing neoplasms arising from chemoreceptor tissue at the heart base in dogs, most frequently reported in brachycephalic breeds; to the authors' knowledge, their occurrence in nonbrachycephalic large breeds, such as the Alaskan Malamute, is uncommonly documented. An 8-year-old intact male Alaskan Malamute (body weight 44.8 kg) was referred with a history of lethargy, inappetence, exercise intolerance, and ascites. Echocardiography confirmed extensive pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade and a multinodular, irregularly shaped heart-base mass invading the left atrium, right atrium, left auricle, and aortic root. The dog underwent two pericardiocentesis procedures, yielding 350 and 630 mL of serosanguinous fluid on Days 1 and 15, respectively. The dog died prior to the scheduled 1-week re-evaluation. Postmortem examination confirmed a multinodular, irregularly shaped, extensively invasive mass involving all cardiac chambers and the aortic root, with histopathological features morphologically consistent with chemodectoma. This case documents a fatal cardiac chemodectoma in an Alaskan Malamute, contributing to the limited literature on heart-base tumors in nonbrachycephalic large breeds, and emphasizes the importance of thorough echocardiographic evaluation, serial imaging in dogs with recurrent pericardial effusion, and counseling regarding a guarded-to-poor prognosis with extensive cardiac invasion.

papers.title: Canine Hemangiosarcoma Cell Lines In Vitro Platform Captures Morphological, Functional, and Molecular Diversity.
papers.authors: di Caporiacco L, Merighi F, Giardino L, Marconato L, Baldassarro VA, Calzà L, Quadalti C
papers.abstract: Both canine hemangiosarcoma and human angiosarcoma are aggressive malignancies characterized by clinical and molecular heterogeneity. Current in vitro models rely on individual cell lines, failing to capture this biological complexity. We established a standardized 2D in vitro platform comprising a panel of three canine primary splenic hemangiosarcoma cell lines (EMN009, EMN011, EMN017) and one patient-matched brain metastasis (EMN010) evaluated in parallel. Using gold-standard assays-morphometrics, growth, migration and tube-formation assays-alongside disease-relevant transcriptomic and microRNA profiling, we characterized this multi-line system under harmonized conditions. Neoplastic lines shared a robust core angiogenic signature of 42 overexpressed genes linked to VEGF, AGE-RAGE, and S1P signaling, and a 47-gene cancer stem cell engine enriched in the Hippo/YAP1 pathway. Transcriptomic clustering divided the lines into slower-growing primary tumors (EMN009/EMN011) and highly angiogenic phenotypes (EMN017/EMN010). Isogenic comparison revealed that the metastatic EMN010 uniquely upregulates STAT signaling and peptidyl-tyrosine phosphorylation. MicroRNA profiling demonstrated a global downregulation of tumor-suppressors miR-126-5p and miR-452-5p, unleashing VEGFA-driven angiogenesis, while visceral hemangiosarcoma biomarker miR-214-3p was significantly upregulated. Conversely, miR-10b and miR-133-3p expression varied across lines, reflecting ongoing clonal evolution. This integrated platform successfully recapitulates hemangiosarcoma heterogeneity, providing a reliable, standardized framework for comparative oncology and targeted pathophysiological studies.

papers.title: Comparison of an Anti-α(v)β(3) Integrin NIR Fluorescent Probe and Indocyanin Green for Precision Resection of Naturally Occurring Sarcomas in Dogs-A Randomized Blinded Case-Controlled Pilot Study.
papers.authors: Nolff MC, Grest P, Seehusen F, Beer P
papers.abstract: The infiltrative growth of sarcomas represents a challenge for complete resection, as tumour borders are not easily detectable. Fluorescence guided surgery (FGS) allows improved visualization of tumour margins and could improve resection accuracy. Unfortunately, studies validating the impact of FGS are rare, and direct comparisons of different dyes are not available. Dogs (n = 20) that were presented for sarcoma resection were prospectively enrolled and randomized to either receive indocyanine green (ICG, Group 1) or a targeted anti-αvβ3 integrin probe (Group 2) prior to surgery. FGS was performed in both groups with the surgeon blinded to treatment. The false positive and false negative rates as well as tumour-to-background ratio (TBR) were calculated for each dye. Correlation of fluorescent area and histologically confirmed tumour extension was determined using the Dice Coefficient (DC). The clinical impact of FGS was determined by assessing the rate of rightfully adapted resections. False positive signal was detected in 9/10 dogs in group 1 and 3/10 dogs in group 2. Mean TBR at skin level was higher in group 2 (4.5 and 5.3) compared to group 1, and this difference reached significance in formalin-fixed tissue (5.3 vs. 2.6, p = 0.016). Correlation of fluorescent signal and histologic tumour extent was strong for both dyes (DC group 1 = 0.64; group 2 = 0.78). Resection of additional neoplastic tissue based on FGS was more frequent in group 2 (3/10 dogs) compared to group 1 (1/10 dogs). The initial results of this study indicate that the targeted anti-αvβ3 integrin probe is more tumour selective than ICG in dogs. This pilot as well as the subsequent follow up study are registered at animalstudyregistry.org https://doi.org/10.17590/asr.0000321.

papers.title: Propofol total intravenous anaesthesia carbon footprint compared to inhalational anaesthesia in small animals undergoing lung lobectomy.
papers.authors: Todd H, Nixon R, Ward R, Bowlt-Blacklock KL
papers.abstract: Climate change poses an increasing threat to both human and animal health. The provision of both human and animal healthcare is associated with high carbon emissions, and the use of volatile anaesthetic agents has been demonstrated to be particularly carbon intensive. In human healthcare, the use of total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) has been demonstrated to generate less carbon emissions than inhalational anaesthetic techniques; however, this has not been assessed in the veterinary context. This retrospective study aimed to assess the carbon emissions associated with inhalational anaesthesia and propofol TIVA in client owned small animals undergoing lung lobectomy at a single University teaching hospital. Results Propofol TIVA was associated with significantly less carbon emissions than inhalational anaesthesia in patients that received the entirety of their anaesthetic via a single technique (p < 0.0001). In patients that received a hybrid anaesthetic with portions of inhalational anaesthesia and portions of TIVA, TIVA again generated significantly less carbon emissions when compared to the inhalational portion (p = 0.0005). Conclusions Where clinically appropriate TIVA should be considered as a less carbon intensive alternative to inhalational anaesthesia in veterinary small animal patients.

papers.title: Dogs and cats undergoing surgery for penetrating thoracic trauma have high survival despite frequent complications, and imaging may underestimate injury severity.
papers.authors: Pathak N, Lozano B, Wang YW, Berns C, Ahn R, Singh A, Lux CN, Glamann S, Ham K, Dickerson V
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe clinical and radiographic findings in dogs and cats with surgically confirmed penetrating thoracic trauma and evaluate associations with outcomes. METHODS: This retrospective, multicenter observational study reviewed records from 5 referral hospitals to identify dogs and cats with surgically confirmed penetrating thoracic trauma between July 1, 2010, and July 31, 2025. Inclusion required thoracic radiographs, surgical reports, and perioperative records. RESULTS: A total of 86 dogs and 5 cats were identified. Mean animal trauma triage score was higher in nonsurvivors (7.6 ± 2.4; n = 20) than survivors (5.2 ± 2.5; 71). Radiographic findings included pneumothorax (73.6%), pulmonary contusions (65.9%), and rib fractures (62.6%). Computed tomography findings often identified more injuries. Time from presentation to surgery did not differ in survivors versus nonsurvivors. Lung lobectomy was performed in 24.2% of patients and was more common in nonsurvivors (45.0% vs 18.3%). Intra- and postoperative complications occurred in 56% and 51.7% of patients, respectively. Survival to discharge was 78.0% (71 of 91 patients), with a median hospitalization of 3.3 days (range, 1 to 12 days). Among 55 patients with follow up, 11 (20%) had complications related to thoracic trauma. CONCLUSIONS: Surgical management of penetrating thoracic trauma was associated with a high survival rate despite frequent complications. Animal trauma triage is a useful prognostic indicator. Computed tomography may alter treatment plans. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate higher injury severity than anticipated based on routine imaging and examination. Higher animal trauma triage scores were associated with nonsurvival and may provide useful prognostic information. Close monitoring is needed following surgery for penetrating thoracic trauma.

papers.title: Most cats with a spinal fracture or luxation recover locomotion within 8 weeks of surgery.
papers.authors: Severac L, Piot C, Gibert S, Sériot P, Griffeuille E, Cavalerie R, Dunié-Mérigot A
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the surgical management of feline vertebral fractures and luxations, with emphasis on neurological recovery. METHODS: Cats that underwent surgical management of vertebral fractures and luxations, without prior neurological disease, were retrospectively enrolled in this observational study from March 1, 2012, to December 31, 2024. Collected data included signalment, vertebral injury characterization, surgical technique, postoperative reduction, modified Frankel score, and urinary incontinence progression, outcome, and complications from clinical/radiographic follow-up and telephone survey. Descriptive statistics were used to describe outcomes. RESULTS: 30 cats met the inclusion criteria. Injury locations were lumbar (n = 16), thoracic (9), lumbosacral (4), and cervical (1). Preoperative modified Frankel scores were grade 3 (n = 12), grade 4 (8), grade 2 (4), grade 5 (2), and grade 1 (1). Surgical stabilization techniques primarily involved polymethylmethacrylate with screws (n = 18) or pins (9). At 8 weeks postoperatively, 28 cats were ambulatory. In the long term, 23 cats fully recovered. Grade 5 cats did not show neurological improvement. Among the 28 long-term ambulatory cats, 6 had persistent proprioceptive ataxia and all of these had T3-L3 neuroanatomical lesions. Urinary incontinence persisted in 4 cats. Owner assessment of long-term neurological recovery was good or excellent in 27 of 29 cats. CONCLUSIONS: Surgical management was associated with favorable neurological recovery, even when surgery was delayed or postoperative reduction was incomplete. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: In cats with vertebral fractures or luxations, surgical management should be considered an effective option when spinal instability or cord compression is present, providing that nociception is preserved.

papers.title: Trauma, particularly vehicular strikes, causes substantial years of life lost in dogs and cats.
papers.authors: Sullivan CG, Zersen KM, Pidcoke HF, Hall K
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: "Years of life lost" (YLL) describes the burden of a given cause of death on a population by measuring the years of remaining life expectancy at the time of death. The objective of this study was to quantify the YLL due to trauma in dogs and cats. METHODS: In this retrospective descriptive study, fatal traumatic injury data for dogs and cats were obtained from the Veterinary Committee on Trauma registry from September 2013 to April 2025. Life expectancies for cats and 5 size categories of dogs were obtained from previously published life tables. Years of life lost were calculated by subtracting the years lived from the life expectancy. RESULTS: There were 5,980 animals included in this study: 4,083 dogs and 1,897 cats. Traumatic injury resulted in a median loss of 7.03 years in dogs and 8.18 years in cats. This loss equated to 55% of the canine life expectancy and 73% of the feline life expectancy. The traumatic injury subcategories associated with the most YLL were "injured by falling object," "struck by vehicle," "fall from height," "penetrating bite wound," and "nonpenetrating bite wound." American Staffordshire Terriers were an over-represented breed and had a median YLL of 9.51 years, nearly 75% of their life expectancy. CONCLUSIONS: Trauma is responsible for a substantial loss of life in dogs and cats. Blunt traumas, particularly being struck by a vehicle, predominate in the total loss of life years. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Quantifying YLL provides an additional perspective about the burden of trauma in dogs and cats.

papers.title: Suspected acrylamide toxicosis associated with ingestion of consumer polyacrylamide-based hydrogel migraine caps, eye masks, and wraps in 45 dogs.
papers.authors: Wegenast C, Haugen A, Waratuke K, Bader R, Spiegelberg S, Wilt B, Kane M
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe suspected acute acrylamide toxicosis in dogs following ingestion of consumer polyacrylamide-based hydrogel migraine caps, eye masks, and wraps, and to quantify acrylamide monomer concentrations in associated products. ANIMALS: Cases were identified from the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Poison Control's AnTox database (January 1, 2024, through June 1, 2026). Dogs with single product exposures to hydrogel-containing migraine caps, eye masks, or wraps and strong evidence of exposure were included. Analysis focused on 45 dogs with high or medium likelihood of exposure-related effects. CLINICAL PRESENTATION: Vomiting, tachycardia, seizures, ataxia, and tremors were the most prominent clinical signs across cases. Behavior changes were common and included anxiety, agitation, frantic behavior, restlessness, and aggression. In one dog, behavior consistent with hallucinations was described. Panting, hyperthermia, hyperesthesia, hypotension, and lethargy or depression were also reported. RESULTS: The most common clinicopathologic findings were hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and hemoconcentration. Management was supportive and included anticonvulsants, muscle relaxants, IV fluids, and electrolyte supplementation. Among 21 dogs with known outcomes, 14 (67%) died or were euthanized. Analysis of polyacrylamide-based hydrogel samples revealed acrylamide monomer concentrations ranging from 12,900 to 51,800 ppm, substantially exceeding expected residual levels and indicating a clinically meaningful risk of acrylamide monomer exposure. Findings were consistent with acute acrylamide toxicosis. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Consumer polyacrylamide-based hydrogel products contain variable levels of residual neurotoxic acrylamide monomer and represent a potentially life-threatening source of toxicosis.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Evaluation of Left Atrial Reservoir Strain by Two-Dimensional Speckle-Tracking Echocardiography in Cats with Stage B1 Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
papers.authors: Algan D, Varlik T, Bach MBT, Gleerup CH, Yilmaz Z, Koch J
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Left atrial reservoir strain (LA S_R), assessed by two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography (2D-STE), reflects left atrial (LA) function and may reveal subtle alterations in LA mechanics in cats with American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine (ACVIM) stage B1 hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) compared with healthy cats. This study aimed to determine whether LA S_R differs between cats with HCM (stage B1) and healthy cats using 2D-STE. METHODS: Sixty-one client-owned cats were retrospectively identified and included from medical databases. These cats were classified as healthy controls (Stage A; n=30) or preclinical HCM (Stage B1; n=31) according to ACVIM consensus guidelines. All cats underwent a comprehensive conventional echocardiographic examination, including two-dimensional, M-mode, color Doppler, pulsed-wave Doppler, and tissue Doppler imaging, as part of clinical care or screening protocols. Conventional two-dimensional assessment of LA size and function included the LA/Ao ratio, LA diameter, LA area, LA fractional shortening (LA FS), and LA ejection fraction (LA EF). LA S_R was subsequently measured offline using automated function imaging software. Reproducibility was assessed via intra- and inter-observer intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to compare the discriminatory performance of LA S_R and the evaluated LA variables between the predefined study groups. RESULTS: Cats with ACVIM stage B1 HCM had significantly lower LA S_R than healthy controls (19.0% [IQR, 14.5-22.0%] vs 38.0% [IQR, 30.25-42.50%], respectively; P < 0.001). LA S_R reproducibility was high with an intra-observer ICC of 0.974 and an inter-observer ICC of 0.894. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Assessment of LA S_R was feasible in cats with stage B1 HCM. LA S_R values differed between affected cats and healthy controls, with lower values observed in the affected group and good reproducibility. These findings suggest that LA S_R may provide complementary information on LA function in cats with this stage of disease.

papers.title: Age distribution and regression-associated immunophenotypic features in canine cutaneous histiocytoma.
papers.authors: Chen YM, Liao ZW, Kuo CL, Kuo CC, Huang WH
papers.abstract: Canine cutaneous histiocytoma (CCH) is a benign tumor characterized by spontaneous immune-mediated regression. Although common in young dogs, it also occurs in older animals. This retrospective study evaluated histologic and immunohistochemical features of CCH across age groups, focusing on mitotic count, lymphocytic infiltration grade, major histocompatibility complex II (MHC-II) expression score and pattern, and CD206 expression. Cases were divided using an a priori 4-year cutoff based on reported age distributions. Immunohistochemistry was performed for CD3, MHC-II, and CD206, with MHC-II expression categorized by score and pattern (membranous versus cytoplasmic). Thirty-eight cases were included, and the age range was 0.75-14 years (median, 7 years). MHC-II score differed significantly between age groups (P=0.0118), whereas mitotic count, lymphocytic infiltration grade, CD206 score, and MHC-II pattern did not. Age showed a weak negative correlation with MHC-II score (r=-0.3299, P=0.0431). However, multivariable logistic regression demonstrated that age was not independently associated with the membranous MHC-II pattern after adjustment for lymphocytic infiltration grade (OR=1.20, 95% CI 0.99-1.50). In contrast, higher lymphocytic infiltration was associated with membranous MHC-II expression (OR=9.87, 95% CI 1.96-77.54). These findings suggest that, in this cohort, regression-associated MHC-II localization was more closely related to lymphocytic infiltration grade than to age. In conclusion, CCH in older dogs showed largely comparable histologic and immunophenotypic features to those in younger dogs, although age-related differences in MHC-II expression score should be interpreted cautiously.

papers.title: Geometric morphometric analysis of cardiac shape changes associated with myxomatous mitral valve disease in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels.
papers.authors: Bakıcı C, Vurucu M, Kılıçlı İB, Mavili ED, Batur B
papers.abstract: Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) is a progressive cardiac disorder in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels (CKCS), characterized not only by cardiac enlargement but also by complex morphological remodeling of the cardiac silhouette. This study aimed to evaluate stage-dependent configurational changes in heart shape across the American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine (ACVIM) stages (A-D) using two-dimensional geometric morphometric analysis of thoracic radiographs. A total of 54 CKCS dogs (Stage A: n = 9, Stage B1: n = 11, Stage B2: n = 10, Stage C: n = 12, Stage D: n = 12) that underwent both echocardiography and right lateral thoracic radiography were included. Shape data were obtained from ten anatomically homologous landmarks digitized using TpsDig software. Following Generalized Procrustes Analysis in MorphoJ, principal component analysis (PCA), discriminant function analysis (DFA), multivariate analysis of variance using PAST, and canonical variate analysis (CVA) were performed to assess intergroup shape differences. Vertebral heart score (VHS), vertebral left atrial score (VLAS), age, and body weight were compared among ACVIM-classified MMVD groups using the Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn post-hoc tests. The first three principal components explained 78.68% of total shape variation (PC1: 32.55%, PC2: 26.86%, PC3: 19.27%), indicating substantial non-uniform remodeling of the cardiac silhouette. Multivariate analyses demonstrated statistically significant shape differences among groups, confirmed by MANOVA (Wilks'λ=0.673, p < 0.05) and CVA (Goodall's F=6.99, p < 0.001). DFA revealed robust discrimination between disease stages (Hotelling's T²=199.89, p < 0.05; permutation test p < 0.001), with the most pronounced differences observed between stages B2 and D (p < 0.001), as well as between preclinical stages B1 and B2 (p < 0.05). Furthermore, both VHS (H=45.09, p < 0.001) and VLAS (H=39.98, p < 0.001) significantly differed across stages, with VLAS showing a significant distinction between preclinical stages B1 and B2 (p < 0.05). Shape changes were characterized by non-homogeneous expansion of the left atrial border, craniodorsal displacement of the cardiac apex, and progressive globular remodeling of the heart silhouette. These findings demonstrate that radiographic geometric morphometrics provide a sensitive and objective framework for identifying clinically relevant morphological transitions in MMVD, particularly at the critical therapeutic decision threshold between ACVIM stages B1 and B2. Geometric morphometric analysis may therefore serve as a valuable complementary tool in the radiographic assessment and staging of MMVD in CKCS dogs.

papers.title: Effect of thoracic duct identification by CT lymphangiography and intraoperative contrast on surgical outcome in cats with idiopathic chylothorax.
papers.authors: Andrews C, Case JB, Burneko M, Thieman K, Williams RW, Ham K, Solari FP, Lubanski JM, Vilaplana-Grosso FR
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To report the success of thoracic duct (TD) enhancement in cats with idiopathic chylothorax on preoperative computed tomography lymphangiography (CTLA) and intraoperative TD colorization (IOC), and to compare surgical outcomes between cats that did and did not have successful pre- and intraoperative TD enhancement. STUDY DESIGN: Multi-institutional retrospective study. ANIMALS: A total of 24 cats undergoing preoperative CTLA, IOC and TD ligation between February 2016 and January 2025. METHODS: Signalment, preoperative diagnostics, method of iohexol administration and quality of TD enhancement on CTLA, surgical procedure, success of TD enhancement via intraoperative colorization, postoperative complications, and clinical outcome were reviewed. RESULTS: TD enhancement on CTLA was successful in 70.8% of cats, with similar quality of enhancement appreciated with metatarsal and popliteal iohexol injection. TD colorization with indocyanine green (ICG) seen via near-infrared fluorescence (NIRF) was successful in four of five (80%) cats, while methylene blue was successful in eight of 15 (53%) cats. When both TD enhancement on CTLA and IOC occurred, clinical resolution rates were highest (77%) and significantly longer survival times were observed (p = .002), compared to when either CTLA or IOC (53%) or neither (25%) was successful. CONCLUSION: Successful enhancement of the TD via CTLA and IOC led to higher clinical resolution rates and was associated with longer survival compared to when only one or neither modality was successful. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: The success of TD enhancement via CTLA and IOC may have prognostic significance for cats with idiopathic chylothorax.

papers.title: Influence of Breed on Tracheal Diameter and Endotracheal Tube Size Selection in Dogs: A Retrospective Analysis.
papers.authors: Kim J, Lee I, Son WG, Lee I, Kim H
papers.abstract: Selecting the correct endotracheal tube (ETT) size is critical for safe anesthesia in dogs. Current ETT size recommendations are largely based on body weight (BW), although some breeds, particularly brachycephalic dogs, may receive smaller ETTs than predicted from BW alone. This two-part retrospective study was performed to evaluate the effect of breed on ETT selection. In Part 1, computed tomography (CT)-measured tracheal diameters (TD) were compared among five small dog breeds weighing 4-5 kg and having a body condition score of 5/9. In Part 2, an expanded clinical cohort of 512 dogs from eight breeds was used to compare clinically selected ETT sizes with BW-based predictions. Statistical models assessed whether breed influenced clinically used ETT sizes after accounting for body mass using the cube root of BW. CT measurements revealed that TD differed significantly among breeds within a similar body-weight range. In the Part 2 clinical cohort, clinically selected ETT size was significantly associated with breed, the cube root of BW, and their interaction. Shih Tzus, French Bulldogs, Pekingese, and Boston Terriers had clinically selected ETT sizes smaller than BW-based predicted sizes, with a median discrepancy of approximately 0.5 mm in Shih Tzus and approximately 1.0 mm in French Bulldogs, Pekingese, and Boston Terriers. These findings suggest that the magnitude of discrepancy from BW-based predictions varies among brachycephalic breeds, indicating that breed may warrant consideration when estimating ETT size.

papers.title: Veterinary point-of-care ultrasound probe orientation and location for detection of pleural effusion in canine cadavers: a pilot study.
papers.authors: Di Franco C, Menard J, Romero A, Chalhoub S, Madden V, Boysen SR
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether point-of-care ultrasound probe location (at or below the costochondral junction) and probe orientation (perpendicular or parallel to the ribs) affect operator ability to detect pleural effusion in a canine cadaver model. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Twelve intubated canine cadavers with scant to large volume pleural effusion were scanned in sternal recumbency while receiving positive pressure ventilation. Twelve operators (2 emergency and critical care specialists, 2 veterinary students and 8 interns) performed blinded bilateral thoracic point-of-care ultrasound using two randomised scanning protocols: a modified TFAST for pleural fluid technique and a modified Calgary PLUS for pleural fluid technique. Hemithoraces were categorised as scant-to-mild or moderate-to-large effusion for statistical analysis. Paired detection rates were compared using McNemar's test. RESULTS: Overall detection of pleural effusion was significantly higher using the modified Calgary PLUS for pleural fluid technique compared with the modified TFAST for pleural fluid technique (89.1% vs. 60.9%; P < .001). There was a statistically significant increase in the detection of scant-to-mild effusion with the modified Calgary PLUS for pleural fluid technique (84.4% vs. 37.5%; P < .001). No significant difference was observed for moderate-to-large effusions (93.8% vs. 84.4%; P = .25). CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: The site assessed and probe orientation used with different thoracic point-of-care ultrasound protocols can influence the operator's ability to detect pleural effusion in positive pressure ventilation canine cadavers placed in sternal recumbency. Incorporating a probe orientation that is parallel to the ribs in the more ventral regions of the thorax during point-of-care ultrasound may improve the operator's detection of pleural effusions, particularly when smaller volumes of pleural fluid are present.

papers.title: Ventilatory compensation for metabolic acidosis is independent of hypertension in dogs with chronic kidney disease.
papers.authors: da Silva Rueda L, Pessina ALR, Senhorello ILS, Franco RP, Dos Santos PSP, Dias MVM, Gomes LF, Ferreira WL
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Metabolic acidosis is common in dogs with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and induces ventilatory compensation. Systemic arterial hypertension frequently accompanies CKD, but its influence on the ventilatory response remains unclear. METHODS: This ambispective observational study included 42 dogs with CKD and metabolic acidosis. Venous partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2) was compared between normotensive (systolic blood pressure [SBP] < 150 mmHg) and hypertensive (SBP ≥ 150 mmHg) dogs. Pearson's correlation and multiple linear regression were used to evaluate base excess (BE), SBP and serum creatinine as predictors of venous PCO2. RESULTS: Metabolic acidosis severity (BE) was associated with ventilatory response (PCO2) (p < 0.001), whereas SBP showed no association. Mean PCO2 did not differ between normotensive and hypertensive dogs (p = 0.373). Serum creatinine independently predicted PCO2 (p < 0.001), with higher concentrations associated with higher PCO2. LIMITATIONS: The observational design, limited sample size and incomplete International Renal Interest Society staging may limit the generalisability of the findings. CONCLUSION: In dogs with CKD and metabolic acidosis, ventilatory compensation, assessed by venous PCO2, was primarily associated with the severity of the metabolic disturbance and showed no significant association with blood pressure status. Compensation may be attenuated as azotaemia worsens.

papers.title: Computed tomography perfusion parameters may aid preoperative differentiation of canine pheochromocytomas from adrenocortical tumors.
papers.authors: Iida K, Ishigaki K, Ishikawa C, Shiozawa N, Kinpara M, Hayakawa T, Yamaoka S, Yamada N, Wang P, Yoshida O
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To characterize CT perfusion (CTP)-derived time to highest observed adrenal tissue enhancement (T-peak) and arterial blood flow (AF), evaluate associations with triple-phase CT findings, and assess the diagnostic performance of T-peak, AF, and the tumor-to-contralateral adrenal AF ratio for differentiating pheochromocytomas from adrenocortical tumors. METHODS: Historical CTP data from 5 healthy Beagles served as controls. Client-owned dogs evaluated from November 21, 2024, through May 31, 2026, underwent triple-phase CT, CTP, adrenalectomy, and histopathology. Time to highest observed adrenal tissue enhancement was the interval from contrast administration to the greatest sampled adrenal attenuation; AF was calculated with a single-input maximum-slope model. RESULTS: 20 dogs with 22 tumors (8 adrenocortical adenomas, 7 adrenocortical carcinomas, and 7 pheochromocytomas [PHEOs]) were included. Time to highest observed adrenal tissue enhancement was longer in both adrenocortical tumor groups than in PHEOs; a post hoc cutoff < 36.0 seconds yielded apparent 100% sensitivity and specificity. Arterial blood flow was lower in both adrenocortical tumor groups than in controls and higher in PHEOs than in adrenocortical carcinomas. Arterial blood flow had an area under the curve of 0.923; a cutoff > 100.60 mL/min/100 mL yielded apparent 85.7% sensitivity and 100% specificity. Among 17 dogs with unilateral tumors, the tumor-to-contralateral AF ratio completely separated PHEOs from adrenocortical tumors. Arterial blood flow correlated positively with CT wash-in and washout indices, whereas T-peak correlated negatively with arterial- and venous-phase percentage enhancement washout. CONCLUSIONS: Time to highest observed adrenal tissue enhancement and AF differed among adrenal tumor types and were associated with CT enhancement characteristics. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Computed tomography perfusion may provide adjunctive information for preoperative adrenal tumor characterization, but the proposed thresholds require validation in larger independent cohorts.

papers.title: Is 28 days of doxycycline still justified for canine Lyme arthropathy? A call for a randomized controlled trial.
papers.authors: Emdin F, Daneman N, Weese JS
papers.abstract: Canine Lyme borreliosis is commonly treated with a 28-day course of doxycycline, a regimen based on historical precedent rather than evidence. Most dogs exposed to Borrelia burgdorferi remain clinically normal despite seroconversion; of those that do develop clinical Lyme disease, the most common presentation is acute or recurrent shifting-leg lameness consistent with Lyme arthropathy. This Viewpoint proposes there is clinical equipoise to evaluate shorter durations of 10 days of doxycycline in dogs with uncomplicated Lyme arthropathy and outlines a prospective parallel-group randomized controlled trial to reassess treatment duration. Determining whether a shorter treatment course is clinically effective also has important implications for antimicrobial stewardship by minimizing unnecessary antimicrobial exposure and selection pressures for antimicrobial resistance.

papers.title: Case Report: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt for management of syringomyelia and Chiari-like malformation in a Cavalier King Charles Spaniel.
papers.authors: Fernandez Cid A, Tabanez J, Black C, Rusbridge C
papers.abstract: A 1-year-old male Cavalier King Charles Spaniel (CKCS) was presented with spinal hyperesthesia, reluctance to exercise, and phantom scratching. MRI revealed a Chiari-like malformation (CM) with brachycephaly, cerebellar herniation, ventriculomegaly, and syringomyelia extending from the odontoid peg to L5, with a maximum transverse syrinx width of 7.0 mm at C2-C3. Medical management (meloxicam and gabapentin) failed to resolve clinical signs. Due to significantly increased lateral ventricles and concern for syrinx progression, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed. Aside from transient post-operative pneumocephalus, the procedure was successful. The dog showed significant clinical improvement, and follow-up MRI demonstrated syrinx reduction and resolution of lateral ventricles. At 6 months post-op, the syrinx measured 2.3 mm. Eight months after the surgery, the dog experienced a brief episode of a suspected movement disorder like but recovered fully. The patient remains pain-free and neurologically normal. This case describes the clinical and imaging outcomes of ventriculoperitoneal shunting (VPS) in a dog with Chiari-like malformation, syringomyelia, and ventriculomegaly.

papers.title: Effects of pregabalin added to a multimodal anesthetic protocol in cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy.
papers.authors: Romano M, Hernández-Avalos I, Nanci C, Costa S, Lombardo A, Di Pietro S, Spadola F, Interlandi C
papers.abstract: Advancement in anesthetic protocols is necessary to address the evolving challenges of perioperative cats' management in veterinary practice. In this study, 54 cats were enrolled and were randomly assigned to either Group P (Pregabalin, PGB) or Group C (Control). Group P received 5 mg/kg of PGB orally 90 min before hospital admission, while Group C received identical empty capsules. Sedation was assessed using a Feline Multiparametric Sedation Scale and a Simple Qualitative Scale. All cats were premedicated with methadone (0.2 mg/kg IM) and alfaxalone (1 mg/kg IM). Anesthesia was induced with propofol at 2 mg/kg and maintained with isoflurane. Physiological parameters (HR, RR, SpO2, EtCO2, Blood Pressure, and Temperature) were monitored throughout surgery. In the immediate postoperative period, the Glasgow Feline Composite Measure Pain Scale short-form and the Feline Grimace Scale were used, measured at 0, 15, 30, and 60 min after extubation. Statistical analysis included Two-way ANOVA for physiological data and Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney tests for pain and sedation scores. Sedation scores increased in Group P by 2.46 (95% CI: 1.69 to 3.23; p < 0.001). Conversely, the scores of the scales used in the immediate postoperative period were significantly lower in the Group P at all evaluation times -2.15 (95% CI: -2.92 to -1.39; p < 0.001). No significant differences were observed in physiological parameters. In conclusion, prehospital administration of PGB provides effective sedation and improves postoperative comfort, making it a valuable adjunct to feline anesthesia protocols.

papers.title: Assessment of the hepatoprotective effect of a multi-component preparation containing phospholipids, selected amino acids, betaine, and milk thistle extract in dogs with asymptomatic elevation of liver parameters: a pilot study.
papers.authors: Nieradka R, Jank M, Otto S, Kurosad A
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Liver diseases in dogs are often diagnosed at advanced stages due to the organ's high functional reserve. Early supportive therapy with hepatoprotective nutraceuticals may help slow disease progression in dogs with asymptomatic elevation of liver parameters. AIM: The aim of this pilot study was to evaluate the hepatoprotective effect of a multi-component preparation containing phospholipids, selected amino acids, betaine, and milk thistle extract in client-owned dogs with asymptomatic elevation of liver parameters. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Seventeen dogs were included in the open-label study. The animals received Hepatiale Forte Advanced (Vet Expert) for 8 weeks at the manufacturer's recommended dose. Liver enzyme activities (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT), total bilirubin, serum bile acids, hematological parameters, and abdominal ultrasonography were assessed at baseline and after 8 weeks. RESULTS: Supplementation resulted in statistically significant reductions in ALT (p = 0.004), AST (p = 0.004), ALP (p = 0.001), total bilirubin (p = 0.001) and serum bile acids (p = 0.007). A trend toward a decrease was observed for GGT (p = 0.052). Hematological parameters remained stable, and the preparation was well tolerated with no adverse effects reported. Ultrasonographic findings were mostly stable or improved (resolution of biliary sludge in some cases). CONCLUSION: Eight-week supplementation with the multi-component hepatoprotective preparation was associated with significant improvement in liver biochemical parameters in dogs with asymptomatic elevation of liver parameters. The results support further research in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial.

papers.title: Case Report: Epitheliotropic cutaneous presentation of multicentric diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in a dog.
papers.authors: Kim GH, Ko BG, Kim SH, Seo KW, Youn HY, Ryu MO
papers.abstract: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common histological subtype of canine multicentric lymphoma, whereas epitheliotropism is classically associated with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. A 9-year-old neutered male Chihuahua was diagnosed with stage IVb multicentric lymphoma and achieved complete remission with a UW-25 L-CHOP protocol. However, an upper lip mass, cytologically consistent with lymphoma, developed during remission. Electrochemotherapy was performed for local control and resulted in marked reduction of the lesion. The dog later developed recurrent peripheral lymphadenopathy and multiple progressive cutaneous masses despite various chemotherapy protocols and was euthanized at week 59 because of progressive clinical deterioration. Histopathology confirmed diffuse large cell lymphoma in the submandibular lymph node, whereas the cutaneous lesions showed neoplastic lymphoid infiltration with multifocal epidermal invasion, mimicking epitheliotropic T-cell lymphoma. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) confirmed diffuse CD20 expression in both sites, with CD3 labeling limited to scattered background lymphocytes. These findings supported the interpretation of secondary cutaneous involvement of DLBCL with a highly unusual epitheliotropic pattern and emphasize the importance of IHC for accurate immunophenotypic classification of cutaneous lymphoma lesions.

papers.title: Reduced Plasma Cardiac Myosin-Binding Protein-C Concentrations in Cats with Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Evidence from Chronic, Treated Disease.
papers.authors: Tanakwang N, Sakunasing N, Kumphune S, Mektrirat R, Na Lampang K, Boonyapakorn C, Pongkan W
papers.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), the most common cardiac disease in cats, is associated with genetic variants, including MYBPC3, which encodes cardiac myosin-binding protein C (cMyBP-C), a key sarcomeric protein involved in myocardial contractility. Although circulating cMyBP-C has emerged as a biomarker of myocardial injury in humans, its clinical relevance in feline HCM remains unclear. This study characterized plasma cMyBP-C and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) concentrations across different stages of feline HCM, evaluated their diagnostic performance, and assessed their associations with echocardiographic parameters. A cross-sectional study included 65 cats: 25 healthy cats, 25 with subclinical HCM, and 15 with clinical HCM (chronic and treated). Plasma NT-proBNP was significantly higher in clinical HCM than in healthy cats (p = 0.0117), whereas plasma cMyBP-C was lower in clinical HCM than in subclinical HCM (p = 0.0462) and healthy cats (p = 0.001). At a cut-off of <1.270 ng/mL, plasma cMyBP-C showed 76.19% sensitivity and 65.38% specificity for distinguishing HCM. NT-proBNP alone showed higher overall diagnostic accuracy (76.67%) than the combined use of cMyBP-C and NT-proBNP. Neither plasma NT-proBNP nor cMyBP-C correlated significantly with echocardiographic parameters. Reduced circulating cMyBP-C concentrations in cats with chronic, treated HCM suggest a biomarker pattern distinct from that reported in acute myocardial injury and warrant further investigation.

papers.title: An observational study investigating the efficacy of heated general anaesthetic circuits during feline flank ovariohysterectomies.
papers.authors: Attwood E, Smith K, Loftus L
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: This pilot observational study evaluated the efficacy of the Humphrey ADE-heated general anaesthetic circuit (HGAC) in reducing perioperative inadvertent hypothermia (PIH) by assessing its mitigation of thermal decline in feline patients undergoing flank ovariohysterectomies (OVHs) under general anaesthesia (GA). METHODS: Perioperative rectal temperatures (RTemps) were collected from 20 cats undergoing OVH, with randomised allocation to either the standard general anaesthetic circuit (SGAC; control group) or the HGAC (experimental group). Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS. RESULTS: The mean perioperative RTemps did not differ significantly between the HGAC and SGAC groups across the entire perioperative period. However, from 35 minutes onwards, RTemps were higher in the HGAC group than in the SGAC group, although the difference was not significant (p = 0.066). RTemps in the HGAC group fluctuated less and increased significantly and gradually as GA progressed (phase 2-3: p = 0.016; phase 1-3: p = 0.011), whereas RTemps in the SGAC group decreased significantly (phase 1-3: p = 0.034), becoming borderline hypothermic at approximately 50 minutes of operating time. LIMITATIONS: The study was limited by its small sample size, which is consistent with a pilot study, and by the involvement of multiple veterinary surgeons in performing the procedures. CONCLUSION: HGACs may be beneficial tools warranting further investigation in modern veterinary practice, with the potential to improve patient welfare standards by promoting normothermia.

papers.title: Case Report: Therapeutic plasma exchange for systemic centipede envenomation in a 2-kg Chihuahua dog.
papers.authors: Tang W, Li Y, Sun G, Zheng C, Gao Z, Li S
papers.abstract: A 2-kg, 8-year-old neutered male Chihuahua was presented after a centipede sting to the interdigital region of the right forepaw, followed by lameness and red urine. Wound care and intravenous fluid therapy were provided at the referring clinic; however, pigmenturia persisted and systemic manifestations developed, prompting referral. On admission, the dog had icteric mucous membranes, mild dehydration, and clinicopathologic evidence of systemic inflammation, tissue injury, hepatocellular damage, and suspected hemolysis. Because of the acute systemic manifestations following envenomation and persistence of clinical abnormalities despite initial medical management, membrane-based therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) was performed. Estimated plasma volume was 96 mL, and the prescribed exchange volume was 134 mL (1.4 plasma volumes). Approximately 1,080 mL of whole blood was processed over 3 h. The 68-mL extracorporeal circuit was primed with whole blood, anticoagulation was achieved with heparin, and fresh frozen canine plasma was used as the replacement fluid. TPE was completed over 3 h at a whole blood flow rate of 6 mL/min; transient asymptomatic ionized hypocalcemia was detected and treated with calcium gluconate. After treatment, C-reactive protein decreased from 8.9 to 1.5 mg/dL and appetite returned, although depression initially persisted. The dog subsequently improved during hospitalization and was discharged after 7 days. In this dog, membrane-based TPE was well tolerated despite the small body size and was temporally associated with improvement in clinical signs.

papers.title: Tibial plateau leveling osteotomy surgical site infections: A systematic review with meta-analysis of prevalence and associated risk factors.
papers.authors: Bidjarano AC, Gordon-Evans W, Thomson C
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine the overall prevalence of surgical site infection (SSI) following tibial plateau leveling osteotomy (TPLO) in dogs and to evaluate associated risk factors across published studies. STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review with meta-analysis. SAMPLE POPULATION: Client-owned dogs that underwent TPLO as described in the published literature. METHODS: A systematic review of studies reporting SSI following TPLO was conducted using PRISMA guidelines. Included studies were screened for quality, and pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were performed. For risk factors, pooled ORs were calculated only when ≥3 comparable studies reported ORs with CIs (weight and postoperative antimicrobial administration). RESULTS: The meta-analysis included 30 studies encompassing 8820 dogs (9576 TPLOs). Only 5/30 studies were considered level I or II and then further divided into moderate and high level of evidence. The overall SSI rate, including superficial and deep infections, was 9.11% (range: 2.9%-25.9%) and an explant rate of 4.11% (range: 0%-33.36%). Heterogeneity was moderate to high across studies. In pooled analyses limited to comparable studies, postoperative antimicrobial administration was associated with lower odds of SSI, while bodyweight showed minimal association with SSI risk; both findings should be interpreted cautiously given limited comparability across studies. CONCLUSION: TPLO SSI rates are higher than other clean orthopedic procedures. Current literature is mostly retrospective in nature. These findings emphasize the need for standardized reporting and infection prevention strategies in clinical practice. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: While higher-quality (higher-level) evidence is needed, trends seen in this large population can be used to start quality control measures in hospitals to reduce TPLO SSI rates.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Modified transcanal perendoscopic myringotomy and septotomy technique for cats with otitis media - a retrospective study of 38 cats.
papers.authors: Wetzels BN, Pickee E, Passon M, Den Hertog E, Ter Haar G
papers.abstract: ObjectivesThis study solely aims to describe a convenient minimally invasive technique for access to the ventromedial compartment of the middle ear in cats with polypoid or non-polypoid otitis media.MethodsPatients' records were retrospectively retrieved from cats with otic symptoms. Cats were included based on the presence of fluid/soft tissue within the tympanic cavity on CT imaging, abnormal tympanic membranes on oto-endoscopy and/or abnormal auditory tube openings upon nasopharyngoscopy.ResultsA total of 38 cats with uni- or bilateral bulla effusion and endoscopic abnormalities were included and 43 ears were treated. On CT, all treated ears had effusion of both dorsolateral and ventromedial compartments. Otoscopy revealed an abnormal tympanic membrane in 93% (discoloration in 28%, bulging in 28%, rupture in 16% and a protruding polyp in 21%). On normograde nasopharyngoscopy, the ipsilateral auditory tube was visibly open in 81% and partly or completely obstructed with discharge or polypous material in 19%. A transcanal perendoscopic myringotomy and septotomy using a 1-mm rigid Frazier suction tube was performed in all cases. During treatment, inflammation of the mucosal lining in the bulla was seen in all ears, with intracavital polyp formation in 33%, which was subsequently perendoscopically debrided. All cats were treated with a 7-day course of doxycycline and a tapering course of prednisolone. No procedure-related complications were seen intra- or postoperatively to discharge.Conclusion and relevanceTranscanal perendoscopic myringotomy and septotomy in cats is a rapid, minimally invasive and apparently safe technique which allows access to both compartments of the feline middle ear. Short- and long-term outcome have to be evaluated in future research.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Echocardiographic prevalence and attachment-site patterns of left ventricular bands in cats.
papers.authors: Van den Noortgate G, Zablotski Y, Wess G
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo determine the echocardiographic prevalence and attachment-site patterns of left ventricular bands (LVBs) in cats and assess whether LVB counts differed by sex, sedation status, or echocardiographic group.MethodsIn this prospective observational study, 200 cats undergoing complete transthoracic echocardiographic examination were evaluated for the presence, number, and attachment-site patterns of LVBs. LVBs were defined as discrete intracavitary linear structures connecting two myocardial structures within the left ventricle without insertion into the mitral valve leaflets. Each visible connection was classified according to predefined attachment-site categories. For the phenotype comparison, cats with normal LV wall thickness or focal insertion-site thickening (n = 89) were compared with cats with a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) phenotype (n = 86).ResultsA total of 884 LVBs were identified. At least one LVB was detected in 199/200 cats, yielding an echocardiographic prevalence of 99.5%. The median number was 4 LVBs per cat (range 0-10). The most frequently observed attachment patterns involved the interventricular septum and papillary muscle or accessory papillary muscle-like structures. Overall, 51.9% of LVBs had at least one septal attachment, and 94.3% involved a papillary muscle or accessory papillary muscle-like structure. LVB counts did not differ by sex (P = 0.47), sedation status (P = 0.26), or between the normal/focal insertion-site thickening and HCM phenotype groups (P = 0.98).Conclusions and relevanceLeft ventricular bands were identified in nearly all cats examined and represent a common echocardiographic finding. Most involved septal and papillary muscle-related attachment sites. Sex and sedation status were not significantly associated with LVB number, and no significant difference was identified between the combined normal/focal insertion-site thickening group and the HCM phenotype group. These findings provide a reference framework for the echocardiographic recognition and classification of LVBs in cats under clinical imaging conditions.

papers.title: Alterations in trace element homeostasis in dogs with parvoviral enteritis.
papers.authors: Bekarer K, Çetin E
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Canine parvoviral enteritis (PE) is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease characterised by severe gastrointestinal disturbances and marked immunosuppression. Despite the critical role of micronutrients in immune responses and recovery, data on trace element concentrations in dogs with PE remain limited; findings across existing studies are inconsistent, and chromium (Cr), manganese (Mn) and molybdenum (Mo) have not previously been investigated in this condition. This study aimed to compare plasma concentrations of essential trace elements in dogs diagnosed with PE with those in healthy controls. METHODS: Plasma concentrations of iron (Fe), copper (Cu), zinc (Zn), cobalt (Co), selenium (Se), Cr, Mn and Mo were measured in 26 dogs with PE and 26 healthy dogs using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. RESULTS: In dogs with PE, plasma concentrations of Fe (p < 0.01), Mo (p < 0.001) and Se (p < 0.001) were significantly lower than those in healthy controls, whereas plasma concentrations of Cu, Zn, Cr, Co and Mn did not differ significantly between groups (p > 0.05). LIMITATIONS: The findings should be interpreted in light of several limitations, including the single-time-point sampling design, variation in disease severity among affected dogs, limited availability of detailed clinical data, and the potential influence of individual factors such as age, breed and nutritional status on plasma trace element concentrations. CONCLUSION: These findings provide new insights into the disruption of Fe, Se and Mo homeostasis in dogs with PE. Further studies are needed to evaluate the clinical significance of these changes.

papers.title: Randomised, blinded clinical trial comparing dogs' sedation scores following methadone-medetomidine injection at Governing Vessel 20, the epaxial lumbar muscles or the quadriceps muscles.
papers.authors: Florence H, David Y, Kate W
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intramuscular injection of sedatives into different muscles may affect the quality of sedation. Subcutaneous injection is less painful but has a less predictable effect; however, administration at Governing Vessel 20 (GV20) may improve sedation. METHODS: Seventy-three dogs were premedicated with medetomidine and methadone. The route of administration was determined by random allocation: subcutaneous injection at GV20 (GV-20), intramuscular injection into the quadriceps muscles (IM-Q) or intramuscular injection into the epaxial lumbar muscles (IM-L). Sedation was scored at 3, 7 and 10 minutes after injection using a simple descriptive scale. RESULTS: Scores were higher in groups IM-Q and GV-20 than in group IM-L and did not differ significantly between GV-20 and IM-Q at any time point. Scores differed significantly between IM-L and IM-Q at 3 minutes, between IM-L and both IM-Q and GV-20 at 7 minutes, and between GV-20 and IM-L at 10 minutes. LIMITATIONS: Differences in patient size between groups, inter-rater variability and the use of allometric dosing may have affected the results. CONCLUSIONS: The quality of sedation following injection of methadone and medetomidine at GV20 does not differ significantly from that following injection into the quadriceps muscles, and the injection is well tolerated. Injection into the epaxial lumbar muscles results in less profound sedation, possibly because of inadvertent subcutaneous injection or anatomical differences in tissue perfusion.

papers.title: Long-term CT and US imaging of canine prostatic carcinoma after prostatic artery embolization: a 900-day follow-up case report.
papers.authors: Isshiki S, Tsuji-Kawahara S, Ogata M, Hisamoto S, Hashimoto M, Hasegawa T, Tsunoda I
papers.abstract: Canine prostatic carcinoma is a highly aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis and limited long-term treatment options. Prostatic artery embolization (PAE) has emerged as a minimally invasive alternative, but long-term intraprostatic imaging changes after PAE in dogs remain poorly documented. We performed PAE on a 13-year-old neutered male Chihuahua with prostatic carcinoma. Designating PAE as Day 0, we monitored the prostate, bladder, and lungs with computed tomography (CT), ultrasonography (US), and thoracic radiography for approximately 900 days. Clinical signs remained well controlled; the dog survived until Day 918. CT showed intraprostatic hypoattenuating lesions (Day 33) that enlarged with gas accumulation (Day 173); US showed hypoechoic lesions (Day 271) that became scattered hyperechoic foci (Day 678). Following PAE, the prostatic parenchymal volume decreased by approximately 33% and remained stable until Day 481. No serious PAE-related complications were observed. These findings suggest that PAE induced sustained ischemic, cavitary, and chronic remodeling changes within the prostate, which may have contributed to the prolonged local disease control observed in this dog. To our knowledge, this represents the longest time-course imaging reported after PAE in a dog with prostatic carcinoma and illustrates the potential of PAE as a feasible, minimally invasive treatment option in general veterinary practice.

papers.title: Bleomycin-based electrochemotherapy for recurrent oral CD8-positive epitheliotropic T-cell lymphoma in a dog with durable local control and necrotic regional lymph node changes: a case report.
papers.authors: Akiyoshi M, Hisasue M
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Oral epitheliotropic T-cell lymphoma (ETCL) is an uncommon form of canine cutaneous lymphoma involving the oral mucosa and mucocutaneous junctions. Information regarding optimal treatment strategies and prognosis is limited. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) has demonstrated efficacy against various cutaneous and subcutaneous tumors in dogs and cats; however, reports describing its use for canine oral ETCL are scarce. CASE DESCRIPTION: A 13-year-old male Beagle presented with multiple nodular lesions involving the right maxillary gingiva, buccal mucosa, and mandibular gingiva. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry confirmed CD8-positive epitheliotropic T-cell lymphoma, with more than 90% of neoplastic cells expressing CD3 and CD8. Initial treatment with oclacitinib resulted in a reduction in the size and number of the oral lesions; however, disease progression was observed after 149 days. Bleomycin-based electrochemotherapy (BLM-ECT) was subsequently performed using intravenous bleomycin (20 mg/m2) followed by electric pulse delivery with a four-needle electrode (1,000 V/cm, eight pulses). Two BLM-ECT sessions were administered on days 205 and 238, resulting in marked reduction in the size and number of the oral lesions and prolonged local disease control. On day 354, enlargement of the left mandibular lymph node was observed. Histopathological examination revealed extensive necrosis that precluded definitive determination of lymphoma involvement. Although residual CD3-positive lymphocytes were identified, neither flow cytometry nor polymerase chain reaction for antigen receptor rearrangement (PARR) confirmed a neoplastic lymphoid population. A third BLM-ECT session was performed on day 555 for recurrent erythematous lesions of the median upper and lower lip mucosa, in which T-cell lymphoma was histologically confirmed. At the latest evaluation on day 608, no grossly visible oral lesions were detected, and there was no clinical evidence of systemic dissemination. The dog remained clinically well. CONCLUSION: BLM-ECT provided prolonged local disease control in a dog with recurrent multifocal oral CD8-positive ETCL that had progressed despite oclacitinib treatment. Unusual necrotic changes also developed in regional lymph nodes. The etiology of these changes remained undetermined, and a causal relationship with ECT could not be established. Investigation of pathological and immunological changes following ECT is warranted. BLM-ECT may represent a feasible and repeatable local treatment option for selected dogs with oral ETCL.

papers.title: Repair of a Large Congenital Peritoneopericardial Diaphragmatic Hernia with Canine Small Intestinal Submucosa Patch Reinforcement in a Dog: A Case Report.
papers.authors: Moon TS, Moon SY, Woo SH, Jeong EJ, Park CM, Lee AJ, Kim HY, Kim JM
papers.abstract: Peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic hernia (PPDH) is a congenital anomaly allowing communication between the peritoneal and pericardial cavities. Surgical repair of large diaphragmatic defects can be challenging due to insufficient tissue for primary closure. A 2-year-old intact female White Miniature Schnauzer weighing 6.23 kg presented with a 1-month history of panting and exercise intolerance. Thoracic radiography, ultrasonography, echocardiography, and CT confirmed PPDH with herniation of the left medial and quadrate liver lobes into the pericardial sac. Surgical repair via midline celiotomy revealed a large defect (4.5 × 5 cm) involving approximately 70% of the central tendon. Primary closure was incomplete because only two simple interrupted sutures could be placed at the dorsal margin due to excessive tension, leaving a triangular residual defect larger than 3 × 3 cm at the ventral aspect, which was closed with a two-layer canine small intestinal submucosa (cSIS) patch applied over the residual defect. Reherniation occurred 42 days postoperatively at the margin between the diaphragm and the cSIS patch. At the second surgery, grossly observed tissue presumed to be newly formed self-tissue at the cSIS site enabled direct suture repair. No recurrence was observed during a 5-month follow-up, and a telephone interview with the owner 3 years after the second surgery confirmed that the dog remained free of clinical signs. This case suggests that cSIS may serve as a feasible reinforcement biomaterial for large diaphragmatic defects where primary closure alone is insufficient, although conclusions drawn from a single case remain preliminary, and surveillance for marginal reherniation is warranted.

papers.title: Cannabidiol in small animal practice: current evidence, clinical applications and practical recommendations for dogs and cats.
papers.authors: Sano T
papers.abstract: Cannabidiol has gained increasing attention in small animal practice as a potential adjunctive therapy for a variety of conditions, including osteoarthritis, epilepsy and anxiety-related disorders. This mini-review summarises current clinical evidence in dogs and cats, highlights key limitations and provides practical recommendations for clinicians. Recent studies suggest that cannabidiol may improve pain and mobility in canine osteoarthritis and reduce seizure frequency in refractory epilepsy, although results remain variable. Evidence supporting anxiolytic effects appears more consistent in chronic stress conditions than in acute fear responses. In cats, clinical data are limited, although preliminary studies have evaluated osteoarthritis-associated pain, chronic gingivostomatitis, behavioural responses, pharmacokinetics and safety. Mild adverse effects, including gastrointestinal disturbances and sedation, have been reported in both dogs and cats. Increases in serum alkaline phosphatase activity have been repeatedly reported in dogs, although their clinical significance remains uncertain and monitoring is advisable during prolonged administration. Drug interactions, particularly those involving cytochrome P450 pathways, should also be considered when cannabidiol is administered concurrently with other medications. Overall, current evidence supports cautious, selective use of cannabidiol as an adjunctive rather than primary therapy. While evidence is strongest for canine osteoarthritis and epilepsy, further standardised clinical trials are required to establish optimal dosing strategies, long-term safety and evidence-based clinical guidelines for veterinary practice.
