papers.title: Dedicated Tibial Tuberosity Fixation Plates Provide Comparable Stiffness to Pin and Figure-of-eight Wire Constructs in Ex Vivo Stabilization of Laterally Transposed Tibial Crests.
papers.authors: Shachar O, Milgram J, Ditesheim D, Ben-Amotz R
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study is to compare the ex vivo biomechanical properties of four fixation techniques for stabilizing tibial tuberosity transposition (TTT) in dogs. STUDY DESIGN: Sixteen cadaveric tibiae from eight large-breed dogs were assigned to one of four groups. Groups were defined by the method used to stabilize the transposed tibial tuberosity: two parallel pins (PP), headless compression screw (HCS), two pins with a figure-of-eight wire (TPF8W), and rapid luxation plate system (RLPS). Following completion of the tibial crest osteotomy, the crest was transposed 4 mm laterally and stabilized according to the assigned treatment group. All constructs were loaded to failure via a force applied to the patellar ligament. Stiffness, load and displacement at yield, maximum load, and failure, and work to failure as well as the nature of the failure were recorded. RESULTS: There were no significant differences between the TPF8W and RLPS constructs in median stiffness (84.2 vs. 72.8 MPa), load to yield (778.3 vs. 644.6 N), or load to failure (786.0 vs. 691.2 N), respectively. Constructs stabilized with PP and HCS were significantly less stiff (with median of 61.7 and 47.6 MPa, respectively) and failed at lower loads (with median of 558.4 and 422.3 N, respectively). Failure modes differed among groups: pin bending occurred in all PP constructs (4/4), screw stripping in all HCS constructs (4/4), and patellar ligament rupture in all TPF8W constructs (4/4); RPLS constructs failed by either patellar ligament rupture (2/4) or tibial fracture (2/4). CONCLUSION: TPF8W and the RLPS provided similar mechanical resistance to forces acting on the TTT and were superior to methods that did not engage the distal tibial crest.

papers.title: Case Report: Computed tomographic diagnosis of asymmetric bilateral uterine horn torsion secondary to benign uterine leiomyomas in a non-gravid dog.
papers.authors: Jeong E, Kim J, Kim Y, Eom K, Kim J
papers.abstract: Uterine torsion is uncommon in dogs and most commonly involves a single uterine horn. An 11-year-old intact female Pomeranian was presented with a 2- to 3-day history of abdominal distension, dyspnea, anorexia, vomiting, and oliguria. Clinicopathologic findings indicated renal compromise, electrolyte abnormalities, tissue injury, and marked systemic inflammation. Radiography and ultrasonography revealed large bilateral abdominal masses with peritoneal effusion, although the organ of origin could not be determined. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated masses arising from both uterine horns, with absent central enhancement on the right, minimal central enhancement on the left, and thin peripheral rim enhancement of both masses, suggesting vascular compromise and ischemic injury. Both ovaries showed preserved contrast enhancement, and spiral twisting of both uterine horns and bilateral whirl signs were identified, with the changes being markedly more pronounced on the right. These findings permitted a preoperative diagnosis of asymmetric bilateral uterine horn torsion. Exploratory laparotomy confirmed approximately 1,080° rotation of the right horn around the left horn and 270° rotation of the left horn around its own axis, without gross rupture of the broad ligament. En bloc ovariohysterectomy without prior detorsion and excision of the vaginal mass were performed. Histopathologic examination confirmed leiomyomas of both uterine horns and of the vaginal mass, with extensive hemorrhage and necrosis of the right horn. The dog recovered uneventfully and remained clinically well 9 months after surgery. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first report of bilateral uterine torsion associated with benign leiomyomas in a dog and the first description of bilateral whirl signs on CT in canine uterine torsion.

papers.title: Behavioural and Noise-Level Differences Associated with Response-Independent Treat Delivery in Shelter Dogs.
papers.authors: Vokins P, Ellis JJ
papers.abstract: Animal shelters can be stressful environments for dogs. Undesirable in-kennel behaviours may reflect poor welfare and negatively affect adoption outcomes. Response-independent treat delivery has shown promise for improving in-kennel behaviour, but its effectiveness when delivered by multiple people is less understood. This study evaluated behavioural and noise-level differences associated with response-independent treat delivery in shelter dogs and responses to a subsequent Novel Person. Twenty-four dogs were observed during Baseline and Intervention phases. During Intervention, volunteers delivered treats when approaching kennels. Compared with Baseline, dogs in the Intervention phase were more likely to be at the front of the kennel, face forward, and stand, and were less likely to be at the back of the kennel, face backward, or exhibit prolonged barking. Behavioural changes across and within days occurred primarily during the Baseline. During the Novel Person comparison, several behaviours differed from Trial 4 during Baseline, while standing increased during Intervention. Because Baseline always preceded Intervention, phase was confounded with time, and the observed differences cannot be attributed unequivocally to treat delivery. The observed phase-associated differences in dogs' in-kennel presentation appeared context-dependent and should not be interpreted as a generalized improvement in behaviour or welfare.

papers.title: Effect of mitral valve repair on outcomes in dogs with preclinical myxomatous mitral valve disease: a retrospective cohort study.
papers.authors: Takahashi E, Shimizu S, Kaneko M, Takahashi A, Nii Y, Mizuno M, Kurogochi K, Sawada T, Mizukoshi T, Takeuchi J
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVES: Mitral valve repair (MVR) for myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) in dogs has favorable results, but its effectiveness compared with medical treatment in preclinical (stage B2) dogs remains unclear. This study investigated whether MVR improves survival in preclinical dogs with MMVD. ANIMALS, MATERIALS, AND METHODS: Dogs diagnosed with stage B2 MMVD between October 2016 and September 2020 were divided into an MVR group and a control group receiving medical treatment. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality and the first onset of pulmonary edema. The waiting period between diagnosis and surgery in the MVR group was adjusted as a time-dependent exposure, and survival analysis was performed. RESULTS: Overall, 91 and 171 dogs were enrolled in the MVR and control groups, respectively. The median observation period was 599.5 days (lower and upper quartiles: 374.0-1001.5). The primary outcome occurred in 10 dogs (11.0%) in the MVR group and 69 dogs (40.4%) in the control group. Cox proportional hazards analysis adjusted for time-dependent exposure yielded hazard ratios of 0.12 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.05-0.25, P < 0.001) for MVR and 2.85 (95% CI: 1.69-4.80, P < 0.001) for diuretic use. STUDY LIMITATIONS: Limitations include potential selection bias, limited survey response rate, inter-observer variability in diagnostic assessment, and a short follow-up period. CONCLUSIONS: Dogs undergoing MVR had a lower risk of reaching the composite endpoint than medically managed dogs. These findings may assist veterinarians and owners in decision-making regarding MVR for stage B2 dogs.

papers.title: Pathologic Characterization and Clinical Significance of Lymphovascular Invasion in Canine Thyroid Carcinomas.
papers.authors: Griffin MA, Stoyle B, Oakes A, Flesner B, Lenz JA, Stefanovski D, Durham AC
papers.abstract: The association between lymphovascular invasion (LVI) and outcomes in dogs with thyroid carcinoma is inadequately described, and a standardized definition of LVI is lacking. This study's objectives were to histopathologically and immunohistochemically characterize LVI and to evaluate associated clinical outcomes in dogs with thyroid carcinoma. Inclusion criteria were: dogs that underwent thyroidectomy for thyroid carcinoma with available histopathology samples, and a minimum of 1-year postoperative follow-up data or follow-up to death. Thirty dogs with 35 distinct tumours, including 26 follicular and nine medullary, were evaluated. LVI was characterized as intracapsular endothelialized tumour emboli (without adhered fibrin) in 26 samples, intracapsular tumour emboli with adhered fibrin in seven samples, extracapsular tumour emboli without adhered fibrin in 10 samples, and extracapsular tumour emboli with endothelial disruptions and adhered fibrin in three samples. CD31 and Prox1 positive vessels contained endothelialized tumour thrombi in 17 and one sample, respectively. Extracapsular invasion with (non-endothelialized) and without (endothelialized) associated fibrin were associated with a 10-fold (p = 0.001) and 3-fold (p = 0.013) increase in the likelihood of death, respectively. No significant difference in the likelihood of death was noted between cases of extracapsular invasion with or without fibrin (p = 0.31). Intracapsular tumour thrombi with or without associated fibrin and non-endothelialized tumour thrombi were not associated with outcomes in this cohort. These results support that in dogs with thyroid carcinoma, extracapsular LVI with or without associated fibrin thrombi, but not intracapsular LVI, is associated with worse outcomes. Further study is warranted on a larger population of dogs with standardized treatment and follow-up.

papers.title: Electrochemotherapy achieves high local control of lingual and tonsillar tumors in dogs and cats.
papers.authors: Vizcay J, Portillo F, Sabella T, Diaz M, Impellizeri J, Maglietti F, Tellado M
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe local response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) in dogs and cats with lingual or tonsillar tumors treated with electrochemotherapy (ECT) alone or combined with surgery. METHODS: Medical records were retrospectively reviewed for dogs and cats with a histologically or cytologically confirmed tumor of the tongue or tonsil treated with ECT alone or combined with surgery, with ≥ 1 posttreatment follow-up. Twenty-nine client-owned animals, 7 dogs and 7 cats with lingual tumors and 15 dogs with tonsillar tumors, were included. Response was assessed by modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors; PFS and OS were estimated by Kaplan-Meier analysis. RESULTS: In dogs with lingual tumors, the objective response rate (ORR) was 85.7% (complete response [CR], 71.4%); the median OS was 270 days, with 2 dogs alive at 980 and 1,090 days, and the median PFS was 263 days. In cats with lingual tumors, the ORR was 71.4% (CR, 57.1%), the median OS was 240 days, and all cats died, most of local progression; the median PFS was 215 days. In dogs with tonsillar tumors, the ORR was 80.0% (CR, 66.7%), the median OS was 240 days, and all dogs died, predominantly of pulmonary metastasis; the median PFS was 210 days. CONCLUSIONS: ECT can provide high local response rates in dogs and cats with lingual tumors. In dogs with tonsilar tumors, even when high local response rates are achieved, patients die predominantly from distant metastasis, warranting a multimodal treatment aproach. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: ECT achieved high local response rates in all groups. It appears most useful for function-preserving treatment for lingual tumors. The combination with surgery allows treatment of larger tumors than ECT alone. The survival of dogs with tonsillar tumors was limited by metastatic dissemination, supporting a multimodal approach.

papers.title: Urine Molecular Fingerprinting: exploratory study of a promising technology for detecting cancer and nonneoplastic disease in dogs.
papers.authors: Robertson J, Issa AS, Dervisis N, McGuire K, Tuohy J, Rossmeisl J, Marine B, Jodar L, Marconato L, Fonseca-Alves C
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe a novel technology, Urine Molecular Fingerprinting (UMF), for analyzing the composition of urine and its application for neoplastic/nonneoplastic diseases in dogs. METHODS: Voided urine samples from clinically healthy Bernese Mountain Dogs (n = 263), Golden Retrievers (214), West Highland White Terriers (79), German Shepherd Dogs (21), and other breeds (245). Samples were analyzed using Raman spectroscopy and computational statistics. To illustrate the clinical relevance of UMF, samples from dogs with cancer (n = 142) or nonneoplastic diseases (19) were analyzed and compared with reference UMF databases of clinically healthy dogs. RESULTS: Breed-associated differences in UMFs were present in samples from clinically healthy Bernese Mountain Dogs, Golden Retrievers, German Shepherd Dogs, and West Highland White Terriers. The UMFs of purebred dogs were different from those of a cohort of mixed breed/other purebred dogs. There were no UMF differences associated with age, sex, or neutering status in Bernese Mountain Dogs. The Raman intensity profiles of UMFs from dogs with cancer or nonneoplastic diseases were different from UMFs of clinically healthy dogs. CONCLUSIONS: Preliminary, exploratory studies indicate that UMF is a promising technology for detecting cancer and nonneoplastic disease in dogs. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Urine Molecular Fingerprinting may be useful in the detection of cancer and nonneoplastic diseases in dogs. This technology could be adapted for testing in clinics, supplementing clinical, laboratory, and imaging information used for health assessments. The use of liquid biopsy technology, such as UMF, in canine cancer detection is addressed in the companion Currents in One Health by Robertson et al, JAVMA, June 2026.

papers.title: Feasibility of the ForeSight tissue oximetry system for estimating cerebral and renal tissue oxygen saturation in anesthetized dogs during hyperoxia, normoxia, and hypoxia.
papers.authors: Sakata H, Arai S, Gilleland E, Monnet E
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the feasibility of the ForeSight tissue oximetry system for assessing regional cerebral and renal tissue oxygen saturation in anesthetized dogs across 3 oxygenation states. METHODS: 6 anesthetized Beagles were included. ForeSight tissue oximetry sensors were applied to the cranium and left lateral abdomen to estimate regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rScO2) and regional renal oxygen saturation (rSrO2). The left dorsal pedal artery, right femoral vein, and right jugular vein were cannulated for arterial and venous blood sampling. The distal tips of the jugular and femoral venous catheters were positioned in the renal vein and the most cranial aspect of the internal jugular vein. During hyperoxia, normoxia, and hypoxia, 1-mL blood samples were collected simultaneously from all 3 sites and analyzed using a blood gas analyzer. Weighted reference oxygenation values (REF-CXB) were calculated. Correlation and agreement between REF-CXB and rScO2 or rSrO2 were assessed using repeated-measures correlation and Bland-Altman analyses. RESULTS: rScO2 demonstrated moderate correlation with cerebral REF-CXB (r = 0.70; P < .01) but poor agreement. In contrast, rSrO2 showed no correlation with renal REF-CXB (r = 0.09; P = .62) and poor agreement. CONCLUSIONS: rScO2 demonstrated moderate correlation with the blood gas-derived cerebral oxygen saturation reference estimate in anesthetized dogs, whereas rSrO2 did not reliably reflect the corresponding renal oxygen saturation reference estimate. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Trend monitoring of cerebral oxygenation with the ForeSight system may provide an adjunctive tool for real-time assessment of cerebral oxygenation in dogs undergoing general anesthesia.

papers.title: Tolerability and Outcome of Medical Treatment in Feline Nasal Carcinomas: A Multi-Institutional Retrospective Study.
papers.authors: Amato F, Gobbetti M, Giuliano A, Treggiari E, Pieri M, Bonazzi I, Bianchi ML, Valenti P
papers.abstract: Carcinomas are the second most common feline intranasal neoplasm. Various treatment options, including radiotherapy, surgery or a combination of both, have been described, but data on medical therapy efficacy are lacking. This retrospective study evaluated the outcome of cats with nasal carcinoma (NC) treated with antineoplastic treatment. Cats with a histopathological or cytopathological diagnosis of NC were included. Patients receiving antineoplastic treatment were compared to patients receiving palliative treatment alone. Response to therapy, median time to progression (MTTP) and median survival time (MST) were described and compared for both groups. Analysed clinical variables included the presence of epistaxis, facial deformity, stage, use of NSAIDs and previous surgical debulking. Thirty-three cats were included in the study: 18 in the antineoplastic treatment group and 15 in the palliative treatment group. Forty-eight percent of the entire population had worsening of the clinical signs, 36% remained stable and 16% showed clinical benefit. MTTP of the entire population was 104 days and MST was 178 days. No statistically significant differences were found between groups for either MTTP (96 vs. 111 days; p = 0.95) or MST (197 vs. 262; p = 0.77). None of the evaluated clinical variables was associated with outcome. In this retrospective study, antineoplastic treatment was not associated with a detectable survival advantage over palliative treatment alone. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size and heterogeneity of treatments administered.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Surgical management of type I atresia ani using Heineke-Mikulicz-like anoplasty: a case series of eleven kittens (2022-2025).
papers.authors: Berlemont L, Bondonny L, Massinon J, Chanoit G, Taroni M, Ferrand FX
papers.abstract: CASE SERIES SUMMARY: Type I atresia ani is rare in cats and there is limited published data on the surgical management and prognosis of this condition in feline patients. Appropriate surgical planning requires thorough examination of the rectum, anus, and perineum to accurately diagnose atresia ani and rule out the presence of a rectovaginal or rectourethral fistula. Type I atresia may be treated with balloon dilatation or bougienage but recurrence may occur and several procedures may be required before complete resolution of the stenosis. The objective of this retrospective case series was to describe, for the first time, the clinical application and postoperative outcomes of a Heineke-Mikulicz-like anoplasty technique in kittens with type I atresia ani. The surgical technique was adapted from the Heineke-Mikulicz anoplasty technique described in people. RELEVANCE AND NOVEL INFORMATION: Eleven cats with a mean age of 12.3 weeks (8-20 weeks) were included in this study. Heineke-Mikulicz-like anoplasty was performed in all cases without intraoperative complications. Major postoperative complications occurred in one case (1/11, 9%), with wound dehiscence two days after surgery. However, complete healing was achieved following revision surgery. At long-term follow-up over 13.6 months (6-24 months) no recurrence was reported in 11/11 (100%) cases. While permanent fecal incontinence was reported in 1/11 (9%) cat, long-term outcomes were excellent in 9/11 (81%) cats.These data suggest that Heineke-Mikulicz-like anoplasty is appropriate for the management of type I atresia ani in cats.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Meningiomas in four cats with pseudocystic fluid accumulation including one microcystic meningioma.
papers.authors: Bitoun A, Berthomé C, Frankar H, Fert S, Cauzinille L
papers.abstract: Case series summaryFour cats were presented with progressive prosencephalic signs. An extraaxial mass associated with a pseudocystic component was identified in each case on MRI and pseudocystic meningiomas were suspected. The appearance of the fluid accumulation in Case 1 was more suggestive of an actual cyst, whereas the crescent shaped fluid accumulation was more compatible with subdural fluid accumulation in Cases 2,3 and 4. All cases underwent mass removal through craniotomy and were discharged from the hospital.The meningiomas were classified as fibrous in case 1,2 and 4, and as microcystic in case 3. The fluid analysis in Case 4 revealed a protein rich fluid with neoplastic meningeal cells. Histology of the wall surrounding the fluid in case 4 revealed tumoral meningothelial cells lined against dura mater, without epithelial lining.All cats improved neurologically after surgical removal of the tumour. Follow-up MRI in cases 2 and 3 performed 6 months post operatively identified focal thickening of the meninges in the two cases (2 and 3).Relevance and novel informationThis case series describes four cats with brain meningiomas associated with a pseudocystic component of unknown origin. Including one microcystic meningioma which has not been previously reported in the veterinary literature. The pseudocyst didn't seem to affect the clinical outcomes and postoperative MRI for these four cats.

papers.title: Erythrocyte membrane lipidomic signatures in canine lymphoma: immunophenotype-specific alterations and prognostic associations.
papers.authors: Rinaldi V, Belà B, Porreca A, Fusaro I, Luciani A, Scipioni G, Ferreri C, Gramenzi A, Boari A, Crisi PE
papers.abstract: Lipid metabolic dysregulation is increasingly recognized as a hallmark of cancer. Erythrocyte membrane fatty-acid (FA) profiling may reflect systemic metabolic alterations and provide non-invasive biomarkers of tumor biology. This prospective study investigated the erythrocyte membrane lipidomic profile of dogs with lymphoma and its potential prognostic relevance. Thirty-nine dogs with newly diagnosed lymphoma were enrolled. Clinical staging, flow-cytometric immunophenotyping, and erythrocyte membrane FA analysis were performed at diagnosis. Individual FAs, FA classes, and lipid-derived indices were compared between B-cell and T-cell lymphomas. Lymphoma-specific survival (LSS) was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier analysis and exploratory univariate Cox proportional hazards models. Twenty-five dogs had B-cell lymphoma, and 14 had T-cell lymphoma. T-cell lymphomas were more frequently extranodal, whereas B-cell lymphomas were predominantly multicentric. Palmitoleic acid was significantly lower in T-cell than in B-cell lymphoma. Correlation analysis revealed distinct lipidomic interaction patterns in dogs with lymphoma compared with healthy controls, particularly involving polyunsaturated fatty acids, omega-6 fatty acids, arachidonic acid, and the unsaturation index. The estimated LSS probability was approximately 50% at 180 days. Exploratory Cox analyses identified nominal associations between mixed diet and a lower hazard of lymphoma-related death, higher oleic acid concentrations and a lower hazard, and higher cis-vaccenic acid concentrations and a higher hazard. These findings should be interpreted with caution given the limited sample size, multiple comparisons, and lack of multivariable adjustment. Overall, erythrocyte membrane FA profiling identified immunophenotype-related differences and exploratory associations with outcome, supporting further investigation of lipidomics as a potential prognostic tool in canine lymphoma.

papers.title: Gene electrotransfer for DNA immunotherapy in veterinary oncology: Technical Tutorial Video.
papers.authors: Impellizeri JA, Vigodny A, Sanchez E, Aurisicchio L, Conforti A
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To demonstrate the technique of gene electrotransfer (GET) for administration of plasmid DNA immunotherapy in veterinary oncology. ANIMALS: The method demonstrated in the video is relevant to both canine and feline cancer patients undergoing administration of DNA immunotherapies. METHODS: This Technical Tutorial Video demonstrates patient preparation, IM plasmid administration, electrode positioning, electroporation pulse delivery, and postprocedural assessment for a GET procedure. Required equipment, procedure workflow, and practical technical considerations are reviewed. RESULTS: The video illustrates the general workflow for delivery of plasmid DNA immunotherapy using IM GET under general anesthesia, including patient preparation, plasmid administration, pulse delivery, and patient monitoring. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: GET is increasingly used in veterinary oncology to facilitate delivery of DNA immunotherapies targeting tumor-associated antigens and immunomodulatory molecules. This tutorial provides a practical overview of the technique.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Undenatured type II collagen enhances mobility in cats: a randomized placebo controlled cross over field study.
papers.authors: Piemontese C, Stabile M, Vicenti C, Fracassi L, Lacitignola L, Garcia-Pedraza E, Tesse G, Crovace A, Staffieri F
papers.abstract: Objectives This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a complementary feed containing undenatured type II collagen on mobility and degenerative joint disease (DJD)-associated pain in client-owned cats with mild to moderate DJD. Methods This prospective, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, cross-over clinical study (coded 3361) included twenty cats (13 females, 7 males; mean age 8.7± 3.5 years; mean weight 4.8 ± 0.8 Kg). After Ethical Committee approval (n. 01/2021/DETO) and written informed consent, cats underwent physical and radiographic examination. Cats with confirmed DJD and no significant comorbidities were randomized to receive either undenatured type II collagen or placebo chews once daily for 12 weeks, followed by a six-week washout period and crossover to the alternate treatment. Client-specific outcome measurements (CSOM), the short form of the Feline Musculoskeletal Pain Index (FMPI-sf) and quality of life (QoL) assessments were completed at baseline, 6 weeks and 12 weeks. Results Fourteen cats completed all study visits. Cats receiving undenatured type II collagen showed significant reductions in absolute CSOM and FMPI-sf scores at 6 and 12 weeks compared to baseline (P=0.006 and P=0.009, respectively), reflecting improved mobility and reduced musculoskeletal discomfort. QoL scores improved significantly (P=0.002). After 12 weeks, percentage variation in CSOM and FMPI-sf scores had a higher reduction in the collagen group than placebo (-27% and -30% vs +0.4% and +40%). Furthermore, 57% of cats in the supplemented group achieved a clinically meaningful reduction in CSOM (≥ 2 points) after 12 weeks, compared with 28% in the placebo group. Conclusions and relevance Daily supplementation with undenatured type II collagen improved caregiver-reported mobility and reduced DJD-associated pain in cats with mild to moderate DJD, supporting its potential role as a complementary feed for feline musculoskeletal health.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Pull-out strength of cannulated compression headless screws and cortical screws in the feline sacrum.
papers.authors: Kornmayer M, Klement J, Zablotski Y, Thorwaechter C, Wieser J
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to compare the pull-out strength of cannulated compression headless screws (CCHSs) of two different lengths with that of cortical screws in the feline sacrum. METHODS: In this experimental study, 30 cadavers of adult Domestic Shorthair cats were randomly assigned to three groups: single 2.4 mm cortical screws engaging 60 % of the sacral width (CS 60, n = 10), 2.5 mm CCHSs engaging 60 % of the sacral width (CCHSs 60, n = 10), and 2.5 mm CCHSs engaging 40 % of the sacral width (CCHS 40, n = 10). Screws were inserted into feline sacra and tested for pull-out strength using a universal testing machine at a constant displacement rate of 0.2 mm / sec up to 20 mm. Peak pull-out force (PPF), displacement at PPF and stiffness were calculated from the load-displacement curves and compared among groups using Fisher's ANOVA and the Welch test. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons were performed using Student's t-tests and the Games-Howell test. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. RESULTS: Pairwise comparison of PPF showed significant differences between the CS 60 and CCHS 60 groups (p = 0.05) and between the CS 60 and CCHS 40 groups (p = 0.05). No significant difference was detected between the CCHS 60 and CCHS 40 groups (p = 0.98). For displacement at PPF and stiffness, no significant differences were identified in the pairwise comparison. CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: Fully threaded cortical screws provide greater holding strength than partially threaded CCHSs in cadaveric feline sacra. In addition, a single short CCHS offers holding strength comparable to that of a CCHS of the conventionally recommended length.

papers.title: Chronic renal disease detection developments with future potential to improve veterinary clinical practice.
papers.authors: Arevalo Turrubiarte M, Rideout H, Whetton AD, Geifman N, Armstrong SK
papers.abstract: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a major global human and veterinary health concern. Novel blood and urine biomarkers currently offer significant opportunities to advance early diagnosis, prognosis, and clinical outcomes. Adopting a translational medicine approach, we summarise research performed to date on CKD biomarkers in humans and relate these findings to companion animal CKD biomarker research. Emerging candidates, including microRNAs and multiprotein measurements for diagnostic signatures, are also considered. We discuss the potential complementarity offered by multi-omic approaches and Artificial Intelligence (AI) driven diagnostic algorithm generation for the understanding of CKD pathogenesis in dogs and cats.

papers.title: Analgesic effect of methadone constant rate infusion is not superior to fentanyl constant rate infusion in dogs after spinal surgery: a prospective, randomized, blinded, clinical trial.
papers.authors: Schütter AF, Kästner SBR, Prause B, Tünsmeier J
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to compare the analgesic efficacy of methadone and fentanyl infusions at a 50:1 dose rate in dogs after spinal surgery. METHODS: In a prospective, randomized, blinded clinical trial, 42 dogs with intervertebral disk disease were evaluated at 1, 2, 4, 18, 24, 42, 48, 66, 72, 90, and 96 h after extubation. Based on the treatment groups, the dogs received a presurgical bolus of 0.25 mg/kg methadone or 5 μg/kg fentanyl, followed by an intraoperative and postoperative opioid infusion. In the methadone (M) treatment group, the dogs received 0.2 mg/kg/h methadone, which was reduced stepwise to 0.05 mg/kg/h. In the fentanyl (F) treatment group, the initial dose of 5 μg/kg/h was reduced stepwise to 1 μg/kg/h. Assessments at each time point included a simple sedation score, vital parameters, pain scoring using the Glasgow Composite Measure Pain Scale (CMPS-SF), and sensory testing with von Frey filaments. Multiple Mann-Whitney tests were used for the analysis of CMPS-SF scores and sedation scores. Vital parameters, between and within the groups, were analyzed using mixed-effects analysis and Dunnett's multiple comparison test. The need for rescue analgesia was assessed via survival analysis. The level of significance was set to α = 5%. RESULTS: In the postoperative period, six dogs in group M and four dogs in group F required rescue analgesia. CMPS-SF scores were not different between the groups M and F and did not change significantly over time within the treatment groups. Tactile sensory thresholds were not different between the groups M and F. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Under the dosing regimens investigated, methadone did not provide superior postoperative analgesia compared to fentanyl. From a clinical perspective, both drugs provided effective postoperative analgesia in this heterogeneous cohort of dogs following spinal surgery.

papers.title: Corridor-based relative severity assessment of the canine anaesthetic course.
papers.authors: Kschonek JD, Kästner SBR, Ohland PLS, Lutscher S, Volk HA, Talbot SR
papers.abstract: The Relative Severity Assessment (RELSA) score grades welfare severity based on the magnitude of multivariate deviations from a reference value. Many variables monitored during anaesthesia are homeostatic and become harmful when they leave the normal range in either direction. Building on the corridor concept of the PVS from human intensive care, we conducted a feasibility study to assess the application and behaviour of a corridor extension of RELSA in two canine anaesthesia datasets. Each homeostatic variable was given a normal band, and only its deviation was folded into the standard RELSA algorithm. Severity in this report denotes the number this algorithm returns, and that number has not been shown to represent clinical severity. We obtained two Beagle datasets, including one four-arm within-subject study, allowing a paired between-protocol comparison. This is an exploratory secondary analysis of existing data, with no a priori power calculation. Under the selected bands, the calculated score changed across the recorded anaesthetic course: low while awake, rising at the documented propofol induction, maintained, and resolving on recovery. The dominant departures were hypotension, hypothermia, and mild hypercapnia, sometimes coinciding with a single animal, though their magnitudes are band-dependent. Corridor RELSA produced a number that changed across the recorded anaesthetic course and represented bidirectional departures as a single continuous score. The between-protocol comparison is not interpreted as evidence about the protocols because the verdict it returns depends on the variable panel being scored. The approach is a domain extension and a small refinement of the human-ICU corridor concept.

papers.title: Descriptive Values and Diagnostic Utility of a 13-Lead Electrocardiographic System in Healthy Cats and Cats with Cardiac or Non-Cardiac Disease.
papers.authors: Badric I, Schreiber N, Contiero B, Baron Toaldo M
papers.abstract: Surface electrocardiogram including peripheral limb and precordial leads has shown clinical utility in humans and dogs, but it is rarely employed in cats. This prospective single-center study aimed to evaluate a 13-lead electrocardiographic system including six peripheral limb and seven precordial leads in a group of healthy cats and cats with cardiac and non-cardiac diseases. To obtain 13 leads, after two minutes of simultaneous recording of the first 12 leads, one lead was moved in another position, and two additional minutes were recorded. The aim was to report descriptive values for several electrocardiographic variables from healthy cats and to test the exploratory diagnostic value to identify diseased status. A total of 125 cats with sinus rhythm were enrolled and grouped as healthy (H, n = 40), cardiac disease (CaD, n = 57) or non-cardiac disease without cardiac involvement (NCD, n = 28). Diagnostic work-up included echocardiography for every cat and different additional diagnostic tests based on the clinical need. Cats were mildly restrained in right lateral recumbency, and peripheral limb and precordial leads were positioned according to an adjusted Wilson system. In total 141 electrocardiographic variables were measured by one operator blinded to group allocation. Descriptive values were obtained from the H group. P wave amplitude was generally higher in peripheral limb leads compared to precordial leads. Thirty-five variables differed between H and CaD on pairwise comparison, while no variable differed between H and NCD. On multivariable logistic regression analysis, R wave amplitude in lead II, aVL, and V6, P wave amplitude in V8, and age were useful in identifying cardiac disease in this cohort. The same variables, without age but including R wave amplitude in V8, were also able to discriminate between H cats and cats with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy phenotype. In our population of cats with sinus rhythm, 13-lead electrocardiogram allowed differentiating H cats from those with CaD and with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy but not from cats with NCD. Descriptive values are provided for different variables.

papers.title: Staged caval occlusion enabling en bloc right divisional hepatectomy in two dogs with hepatocellular carcinoma.
papers.authors: Ishigaki K, Asano K
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe staged pre-renal caudal vena cava (CVC) occlusion before en bloc right divisional hepatectomy with segmental caval resection in two dogs with right divisional hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) involving the CVC. ANIMALS: Two client-owned, 11-year-old neutered male dogs (Siberian Husky and Shih Tzu). STUDY DESIGN: Short case series. METHODS: Dog 1 (Siberian Husky) had prior hemoperitoneum and biopsy-confirmed HCC; dog 2 (Shih Tzu) had persistent liver enzyme elevations and a suspected hepatic tumor. Computed tomography (CT) showed right divisional masses (91.8 × 122.3 × 101.4 mm; 77.0 × 94.8 × 70.2 mm) with CVC compression or involvement and no pre-existing collateral venous return. A percutaneously controlled hydraulic occluder was placed around the pre-renal CVC. Gradual outpatient occlusion was performed over 79 and 44 days while monitoring saphenous venous pressure, renal values, and hindlimb edema. Complete CVC occlusion and collateralization were confirmed by CT before en bloc right divisional hepatectomy with segmental CVC resection. RESULTS: Macroscopically complete resection was achieved in both dogs. Complete HCC resection was confirmed histopathologically. Morbidity was limited to transient wound exudation in dog 1 and transient ascites in dog 2. No recurrence or metastasis was identified in dog 1 during follow-up. In dog 2, no clinical signs suggestive of recurrence or metastasis were reported. Survival after hepatectomy was 352 and 2467 days. CONCLUSION: Staged pre-renal CVC occlusion may establish collateral venous return and permit planned en bloc right divisional hepatectomy with segmental CVC resection in carefully selected dogs with right divisional HCC involving the CVC.

papers.title: Computational prescreening of anticancer drugs prior to in vitro validation, primarily in dogs with exploratory cat data, based on cross-species binding conservation.
papers.authors: Lee SW, Kim HY, Choi SK, Lim SG, Ko J, Park J, Baek SM, Park JK, Jang S, Kim C
papers.abstract: Advances in veterinary medicine have prolonged the lifespan of companion animals. As a result, the burden of neoplastic diseases has increased. While targeted anticancer drugs are widely used in human oncology, their clinical translation to companion animals remains limited. Therefore, a systematic framework for prioritizing candidate drugs before in vitro or in vivo testing would be a valuable strategy in veterinary medicine. In the present study, we evaluated the cross-species binding potential of FDA-approved targeted anticancer drugs to canine and feline target proteins. Protein sequence analysis revealed high conservation of drug-binding domains between human, dog, and cat target proteins, with average sequence identities of 97.09% in dogs and 99.12% in cats compared with their human counterparts. Computational docking simulations were performed to evaluate the docking scores between selected drugs and their corresponding target proteins in dog and cat. Most selected drug-target complexes exhibited docking scores comparable to those observed for human targets, and cross-species docking-score correlations were high in both dogs (0.988) and cats (0.996). These findings support the use of docking-based prescreening as a rapid candidate-selection strategy prior to in vitro validation in veterinary medicine.

papers.title: Serum fibroblast growth factor-23 and magnesium concentrations in cats with acute kidney injury: association with disease pathophysiology.
papers.authors: Miyagawa A, Nakano M, Miyakawa H, Miyagawa Y, Takemura N
papers.abstract: Cats with acute kidney injury (AKI) have a high mortality rate and are at risk of progression to chronic kidney disease (CKD). Fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF-23) and magnesium, which are involved in mineral homeostasis and AKI outcomes, may contribute to this progression. This study aimed to evaluate serum FGF-23 and magnesium concentrations at diagnosis in cats with AKI and to investigate their associations with clinical outcomes. This retrospective study included client-owned cats with AKI. Serum FGF-23 and magnesium concentrations were measured at diagnosis, and their associations with AKI outcomes were analyzed. Forty-five cats were enrolled. Serum FGF-23 (P=0.01) and magnesium (P=0.01) concentrations were elevated. Serum FGF-23 tended to increase with prior CKD severity, although differences among CKD groups were not significant (P=0.10). Serum FGF-23 was significantly associated with treatment duration (P=0.008) and changes in serum creatinine during hospitalization (P=0.003), independent of prior CKD status and serum creatinine at diagnosis. A 10-fold increase in FGF-23 was associated with an approximately 47% decrease in the hazard of reaching the lowest serum creatinine concentration. Magnesium was not significantly associated with these outcomes. Measurement of serum FGF-23 at the time of AKI diagnosis may help predict hospitalization duration and renal function decline. Although the role of serum magnesium in the pathophysiology of AKI could not be clearly determined, further investigation of its relationship with FGF-23 may contribute to the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Work outside of work: after-hours use of the electronic medical record among residents at an academic veterinary teaching hospital.
papers.authors: Shah S, Love K, Jenkins D, McCool KE
papers.abstract: The electronic medical record (EMR) is a major contributor to clinician workload, with substantial documentation often occurring outside scheduled patient care hours. In human medicine, after-hours EMR use has been associated with clinician burnout, yet it has not been objectively quantified among veterinary residents. The purpose of this study was to quantify after-hours EMR use among veterinary residents, to compare this across specialties and years of training, and to establish baseline metrics for future studies evaluating documentation efficiency and workflow interventions. EMR login metadata were extracted for 39 residents representing seven specialties at a single academic veterinary teaching hospital between July 2023 and July 2024. Rule-based algorithms quantified weekday after-hours use (pajama time; PJT) and weekend time (WT; weekend EMR use). Repeated-measures hurdle models were used to evaluate associations between specialty, residency year, and after-hours EMR use. Specialty was significantly associated with both the likelihood and duration of after-hours EMR use (p < 0.001). Radiology residents consistently demonstrated the lowest after-hours EMR use, whereas residents in surgery, cardiology, neurology, and small animal internal medicine accumulated substantially greater after-hours EMR time. Among residents who used the EMR during after-hours time, median weekday PJT was 13.57 h/month and median weekend EMR use was 23.38 h/month. First-year residents were more likely than third-year residents to access the EMR during weekday PJT (OR 4.57, 95% CI 1.69-12.36; p = 0.002), although the duration of after-hours EMR use did not differ by residency year. Veterinary residents spend substantial time using the EMR outside scheduled working hours, with marked variation across specialties. Objective EMR metadata provide a scalable, objective approach for quantifying documentation workload and establishes a baseline for evaluating interventions aimed at improving workflow efficiency and documentation practices within veterinary training programs.

papers.title: Surgical management of an unstable occipital condyle fracture in a dog using a patient-specific CNC-milled titanium implant: a case report.
papers.authors: Jeong N, Kim H, Cho C, Jung J
papers.abstract: A 10-year-old castrated male Pomeranian was evaluated after a fall and presented with tetraparesis, dysphagia, and headturn. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a right occipital condyle fracture that caused brainstem compression and cerebellar infarction from a displaced bony fragment. According to the Anderson and Montesano classification in human medicine, this case was presumed to be Type 3, indicating instability, and surgical correction was considered. A bone fragment located in the medulla oblongata was left in situ owing to the potential risk of severe complications from removal. Occipitocervical stabilization surgery was performed to prevent further damage from instability. A patient-specific titanium implant was designed by CAD and fabricated by CNC milling, and screws were applied to the occiput and C1 vertebra using standard techniques, whereas a screw was inserted transversely into the C2 spinous process to minimize the risk of implant failure from neck flexion. Postoperative computed tomography (CT) confirmed proper implant placement without neural injury. Over time, the patient showed improvements in hypoglossal dysfunction and gait, and was discharged on postoperative day five. Occipital condyle fractures are rare in both veterinary and human medicine, with most cases classified as type 1 or 2, and typically do not require surgical intervention. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first peer-reviewed description of surgical stabilization of an occipital condyle fracture in a dog using a patient-specific, CNC-milled titanium implant. Conservative management of occipital condyle fracture and surgical stabilization of craniocervical junction fractures have been described previously, and the contribution of the present report lies in the implant design and fabrication workflow rather than in the surgical management of craniocervical injury per se.

papers.title: Prognostic indicators associated with 2-week survival and postoperative antimicrobial use following ovariohysterectomy for canine pyometra from 2012 to 2021: a multicenter retrospective cohort of 470 cases.
papers.authors: Langfitt SM, Arun A, Spector DI, Maza FJ, Buoniconti S, Regier PJ, Hardie ME, Marvel S, Grimes JA
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to retrospectively evaluate factors associated with 2-week survival following ovariohysterectomy for pyometra in dogs. ANIMALS: This study included 470 intact bitches that underwent ovariohysterectomy for pyometra. METHODS: In this multi-institutional retrospective cohort study, medical records were reviewed for clinical data, including signalment, duration of clinical signs, blood count findings, presence of septic peritonitis, culture and susceptibility results, antibiotics prescribed and duration, and survival at 2 weeks postoperatively (from the medical record or via owner contact). A univariable analysis was performed due to the low mortality rate to evaluate the association between variables and 2-week survival. RESULTS: Four hundred and fifty-two dogs survived to discharge, of which 10 dogs (2.2%) did not survive the 2-week follow-up. Eighteen dogs (3.8%) did not survive to discharge (DNSD). Post-discharge 2-week survival was 97.8% (442/452) and was associated with younger age and the absence of pre-operative azotemia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia (p-values: 0.005, 0.043, 0.004, and 0.015, respectively). No association was found with pyometra type (open vs. closed), oral antibiotic use or duration, or any other assessed variable (p-values > 0.05). CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Younger dogs that were presented for pyometra without azotemia, hyperkalemia, and/or hypoglycemia had improved 2-week postoperative survival. An association between postoperative discharge antibiotic use and 2-week survival was not identified in this study. Further studies with greater statistical power are needed to evaluate the potential effect of postoperative antibiotic use on survival.

papers.title: Prognostic utility of red blood cell distribution width-based ratios and their individual components for mortality prediction in dogs with acute pancreatitis.
papers.authors: Diaz-Gonzalez A, Espadas-Gonzalez L, Pérez-Merino EM, Martínez-Zafra C, Cristóbal-Verdejo JI
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Prognostic assessment is critical in dogs with acute pancreatitis (AP). Composite biomarkers such as the red blood cell distribution width (RDW)-to-albumin ratio (RAR) and hemoglobin-to-RDW ratio (HRR) have shown prognostic value in human critical care but have not been evaluated in canine AP. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted in 80 dogs with AP and 10 healthy controls. The diagnostic and prognostic utility of admission HRR and RAR was compared with that of their individual components measured at admission (RDW, hemoglobin and albumin). Outcome was classified as survival or non-survival to hospital discharge. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis and multivariable logistic regression were performed. RESULTS: The overall mortality rate was 33.75%. Non-survivors presented with significantly lower hemoglobin, albumin and HRR values and significantly higher RDW values than survivors, whereas RAR did not differ between outcome groups. Among the variables evaluated, hemoglobin showed the highest discriminatory performance (AUC = 0.704; 95% CI: 0.583-0.812), followed by HRR (AUC = 0.669; 95% CI: 0.547-0.790), RDW (AUC = 0.663; 95% CI: 0.540-0.786), CAPCSI (AUC = 0.658) and albumin (AUC = 0.634; 95% CI: 0.506-0.757). In the multivariable model including age, hemoglobin, albumin, RDW and CAPCSI, only CAPCSI remained independently associated with survival (adjusted OR = 0.612; 95% CI: 0.403-0.929; p = 0.021). DISCUSSION: Integrating erythrocyte indices into composite ratios offered no clinical advantage over evaluating individual markers in dogs with acute pancreatitis. Among the laboratory variables assessed, hemoglobin showed the highest discriminatory performance, although its overall prognostic accuracy remained moderate. These findings suggest that erythrocyte-derived variables may serve as adjunctive prognostic markers in dogs with AP but should be interpreted alongside established clinical assessment.

papers.title: The Chornobyl Dogs: Why Scientific Evaluation Must Accompany Population Management.
papers.authors: Tuech JJ, Guillin O, Pinson J, Nicolas G, Mousseau TA, Betz JA
papers.abstract: Nearly four decades after the 1986 reactor explosion, several hundred semi-feral dogs persist within the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone. Genomic work has characterised their population structure and shown that radiation-induced mutation does not, on current evidence, drive the differentiation between groups; the cause of that differentiation remains unresolved, and their epigenome has never been examined. These dogs are a potentially valuable model for chronic, low-dose, multi-stressor exposure, not because they are "radiation-adapted", a contested claim, but because they are a human-adjacent, densely sampled, pedigreed mammal for which comparative canine-human tools already exist. Since 2017, a humane sterilisation programme, carried out at the request of and in cooperation with the Ukrainian authorities, has reached near-complete coverage of the established populations. That programme was justified: dogs are formally prohibited in the zone, they injure workers, free-roaming animals inside an operating nuclear facility raise security as well as veterinary concerns, and reproduction was outpacing what the environment could support. Our argument concerns timing rather than policy. The scientific value of this population was never evaluated while it was still breeding, and the archived material that does exist, roughly 400 dogs including parent-offspring trios and repeat-sampled individuals, was assembled for population genetics rather than for the regulatory questions now worth asking. That archive should be analysed for methylation and expression now, as this is the only access to the population as it was. The animals themselves have not gone: several hundred identified dogs are still alive there, so sampling at veterinary contact and the retention of tissue at natural death or clinically indicated euthanasia remain possible, provided they are planned and funded in advance rather than improvised. More generally, the scientific evaluation of a population should accompany the decision to manage it rather than follow it, because sterilisation is not reversible at the population scale and an archive cannot be assembled retrospectively. We set out what such an evaluation requires at the outset of a programme. Its most concrete element asks nothing of the animals: a sterilisation clinic is the only routine access to a free-roaming population under anaesthesia, and the reproductive tissue it removes-the one material capable of addressing germline questions-is discarded as surgical waste.

papers.title: EXPRESS: EFFECTS OF INTRAMUSCULAR AND INTRANASAL ADMINISTRATION OF MEDETOMIDINE ON SEDATION AND SOME CARDIOPULMONARY VARIABLES IN HEALTHY CATS.
papers.authors: Sarra Ferrer M, Faucher S, Didier C, Giry M, Schauvliege S, Verwaerde P, Jourdan G
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo compare the sedative and cardiopulmonary effects following either intranasal (IN) or intramuscular (IM) administration of medetomidine in healthy male cats undergoing neuter procedure.MethodsA total of 26 client-owned healthy cats, aged 7 - 60 months, weighing 4 [3-6] kg (median [min-max]) presented for neutering were included in this blinded, randomized, prospective clinical study. The cats were randomly assigned in two groups to receive medetomidine (40 µg/kg) by IN (16 cats) or IM (10 cats) routes. Sedation was scored during premedication (just before and 10, 15, 20 minutes after medetomidine administration) and during recovery (at the moment of orotracheal extubation, 1 and 2 hours after) with a simple descriptive scale (SDSS) ranging from 0 (no sedation) to 3 (maximum sedation) and a composite scale (CSS) ranging from 0 (no sedation) to 19 (maximum sedation). Heart rate (HR), respiratory frequency (RR), non-invasive arterial blood pressure (NIBP) and haemoglobin oxygen saturation (SpO2) were recorded at the same time points as sedation was assessed.ResultsSedation scores significantly increased for both groups at all time points after medetomidine administration. However, cats in the IM group achieved a higher maximal sedation score and earlier than cats in the IN group (CSSmax 16 [13-17] at TCSSmax 18 [10-20] min versus 14 [9-17] at 20 [15-20] min respectively). HR significantly decreased in both groups after medetomidine administration, but decrease was less pronounced and shorter in IN group. Regarding adverse effects, sneezing, swallowing and vomiting were significantly increased immediately after IN administration.Conclusions and relevanceIN medetomidine (40 µg/kg) can be an alternative, non-invasive route to IM administration for premedicating healthy cats before general anaesthesia for neutering. IN medetomidine premedication produced sufficient sedation with a slower onset and shorter duration but less cardiovascular effects compared to IM in cats.

papers.title: Retrospective Comparison of Gastrointestinal Toxicity in Dogs With Lymphoma Receiving Doxorubicin With or Without Prophylactic Trimethoprim-Sulfadiazine.
papers.authors: Madden EJ, Chan C
papers.abstract: Doxorubicin is commonly used in the treatment of canine lymphoma and other malignancies but is associated with adverse effects, including gastrointestinal toxicity and myelotoxicosis. Previous veterinary studies have suggested that prophylactic antimicrobial administration may reduce chemotherapy-associated toxicity and hospitalisation. However, the potential benefits of prophylactic antimicrobials must be balanced against risks, including antimicrobial resistance and dysbiosis. This retrospective study evaluated the effect of prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfadiazine administration on gastrointestinal and haematologic adverse events in dogs with high-grade multicentric lymphoma receiving doxorubicin for the first time. Medical records from three referral hospitals in Queensland, Australia were reviewed for dogs treated between January 2008 and November 2025. Adverse events occurring within 14 days of doxorubicin administration were retrospectively graded using the Veterinary Cooperative Oncology Group Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events. Sixty dogs met the inclusion criteria, including 21 dogs receiving prophylactic TMS and 39 receiving no prophylactic antibiotics. Gastrointestinal toxicity occurred in 14/21 (66.7%) dogs receiving TMS compared with 13/39 (33.3%) dogs receiving no antibiotics (p = 0.013). After controlling for lymphoma stage, prophylactic TMS administration was associated with a 3.69-fold increase in the odds of GI toxicity (95% CI 1.13-12.11, p = 0.031). No significant differences were identified between groups in severity of GI toxicity, haematologic toxicity, neutropenia or hospitalisation rates. Prophylactic TMS administration during doxorubicin chemotherapy was associated with increased GI toxicity in this cohort, contrasting with previous reports and supporting the need for prospective evaluation of prophylactic antimicrobial use in contemporary geographically distinct canine chemotherapy populations.

papers.title: Quantitative electroencephalographic comparison of intranasal midazolam, intranasal saline, and intrarectal diazepam in healthy dogs: A two-session, fixed-order pilot study.
papers.authors: Musteata M, Ştefănescu RA, Despa A, Borcea D, Charalambous M
papers.abstract: Benzodiazepines are the recommended first-line treatment for canine seizure emergencies, and non-parenteral routes are essential when intravenous access is unavailable. Clinical trials show that intranasal midazolam controls emergency seizures more reliably than rectal diazepam, yet the cortical electrophysiological correlates of these routes remain uncharacterised in dogs. In a two-session, fixed-order (non-randomised) study, the quantitative electroencephalographic (qEEG) profiles of intranasal midazolam (IN-MDZ; 0.2 mg/kg), volume-matched intranasal saline (IN-SAL) and intrarectal diazepam (IR-DZP; 0.5 mg/kg) were compared in six healthy adult dogs. Propofol (1%, 0.5 mL/kg IV) was given in both sessions for electrode placement, and recording followed clinical recovery. Metrics were computed at baseline and 1, 3 and 5 min and analysed with the dog as the unit of replication (n = 6), using Friedman and exact Wilcoxon tests with false-discovery-rate (FDR) control. IN-MDZ was associated with a coherent, rapidly emerging cortical-slowing signature: at 1-3 min it separated from both controls across relative delta, beta, delta/beta, theta/alpha, alpha and entropy, unanimously and drug-specifically, the correlated indices reflecting a single coherent spectral shift reproduced at two time points. This slowing, in contrast to the beta activation reported in seizing human patients, is consistent with a genuine, rapidly acting GABAergic effect, and is concordant with the established clinical efficacy of intranasal midazolam. No contrast survived false-discovery-rate correction; the core indices nonetheless persisted on baseline-corrected change scores (r = 0.7-0.9). The study defines the qEEG endpoints, effect sizes and sample size required for an adequately powered confirmatory trial.

papers.title: Zurich Mini Cementless Total Hip Replacement in Cats: Specific Considerations and Short-Term Outcomes in 11 Cats (17 Hips).
papers.authors: Vedrine B
papers.abstract: Total hip replacement (THR) in cats remains uncommon due to species-specific anatomical features, including limited acetabular retroversion, mismatch between femoral canal and acetabular size, and technical difficulty during femoral preparation related to sclerosis secondary to slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), the main indication in this species. These factors complicate implant selection, canal preparation, and cup orientation. This retrospective study reports clinical and radiographic outcomes of 17 cementless Mini THR procedures performed in 11 cats (nine Maine Coons and two Domestic Shorthairs) between 2022 and 2025. Indications included SCFE (n = 11), hip dysplasia (n = 5), and femoral neck fracture malunion (n = 1). Intraoperative fluoroscopy was used to optimize cup positioning. Two intraoperative complications occurred, consisting of minimal cortical fissures stabilized with prophylactic cerclage wires. Postoperative complications included two femoral fractures (11.8%), one resulting in limb amputation. One traumatic hip luxation occurred 10 months after surgery and was considered unrelated to the procedure. At 8 weeks, all remaining implants were pain-free, stable, and showed complete or advanced osteointegration. With careful planning, intraoperative imaging, and appropriate postoperative management, THR can provide excellent short-term outcomes in cats, although limited implant modularity may restrict optimal fit in some patients.

papers.title: Evaluation of urinary biomarkers for detection of renal tubular injury in Vipera berus-envenomated and critically ill dogs with and without clinically apparent acute kidney injury.
papers.authors: Selin AK, Lilliehöök I, Strage EM, Larsson A, Pelander L
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute kidney injury (AKI) in dogs has high mortality and early diagnosis is essential, but traditional markers are not sensitive enough to detect renal injury in the absence of decreased glomerular filtration rate. The objective of this study was to compare urinary cystatin C (uCysC), N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminidase (uNAG), and glucose (uGlu) among dogs hospitalised because of envenomation by Vipera berus (EVB) or admitted for intensive care without (IC) or with (AKIAPP) clinically apparent AKI, and 30 healthy dogs. Urine and serum samples were collected on days 1 and 2, and urine samples on days 7 and 14. Urinary CysC, NAG, and glucose concentrations were measured with an automated chemistry analyser, normalised to urinary creatinine concentration (uCr) and compared among groups. RESULTS: Ninety-seven dogs were included (30 HC, 28 EVB, 14 AKIAPP and 25 IC dogs). Age, bodyweight, and sex did not differ among groups. On day 1, median [IQR] uCysC/uCr (10-3) and uGlu/uCr were higher (p < 0.008) in EVB (0.05 [0.03-0.11], 0.04 [0.03-0.06)]), IC (0.06 [0.03-0.4], 0.05 [0.03-0.09]), and AKIAPP (4.4 [0.13-30.0], 0.12 [0.05-0.45]) groups, compared to healthy dogs (0.02 [0.01-0.03], 0.03 [0.02-0.04]). Urinary markers decreased over two weeks post hospitalisation in all groups except AKIAPP. Initial levels of uCysC/uCr were higher (p < 0.002) and remained elevated in non-survivors compared to survivors of AKIAPP, suggesting potential prognostic value. CONCLUSIONS: Urinary CysC/uCr and Glu/uCr are potential markers of tubular injury in early stages of AKI in dogs.

papers.title: Oxibendazole induces cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in canine large-cell alimentary lymphoma cells.
papers.authors: Sakai K, Hirao M, Suzuki N, Shimamura S
papers.abstract: Canine large-cell alimentary lymphoma (LCAL) responds poorly to chemotherapy and carries a poor prognosis. We investigated the antitumor effects of oxibendazole (OBZ), a benzimidazole anthelmintic identified by drug screening, in three canine LCAL cell lines. OBZ reduced cell viability in a dose-dependent manner, with half-maximal inhibitory concentration values of 0.08-0.16 μM. Cell cycle analysis showed increased G2/M and sub-G1 fractions, whereas an annexin V/propidium iodide assay demonstrated increased early and late apoptotic cells. Western blotting demonstrated caspase-3 cleavage following OBZ treatment. These findings indicate that OBZ exerts antitumor effects against canine LCAL cells by inducing G2/M cell cycle arrest and caspase-dependent apoptosis and suggest that OBZ may be a candidate for drug repurposing in canine LCAL.

papers.title: Comparison of Ultrasonographic, Radiographic, Computed Tomographic, and Ex Vivo Measurements of Feline Femoral Trochlear Groove Depth.
papers.authors: Silva GPD, Carneiro RK, Mattos MPLDS, Filho FTDA, Brose MM, Alievi MM, Ferreira MP
papers.abstract: Patellar luxation is a common orthopedic condition in cats, and evaluation of trochlear groove depth is important to determine the need for trochleoplasty during surgical planning. This study compared radiography, ultrasonography, and computed tomography with ex vivo measurements, considered the reference method, for the assessment of trochlear groove depth in cats. Twenty-seven stifle joints from 15 healthy adult cats were evaluated. Trochlear groove depth was measured using skyline radiographic projections, ultrasonography with the stifle positioned at 45° and 90° of flexion, computed tomography, and ex vivo evaluation with the stifle flexed at 45° and 90°. Measurements obtained by radiography and ultrasonography with the stifle positioned at 90° did not show significant differences compared with the respective ex vivo measurements at 90°, whereas ultrasonography performed at 45° and computed tomography differed. The results obtained by radiography and ultrasonography at 90° suggest that these techniques provide reliable estimates of trochlear groove depth in healthy cats. These findings support the use of radiography and ultrasonography as reliable imaging methods for preoperative evaluation and surgical planning in cats with patellar luxation.

papers.title: Right-to-left shunting following left atrial decompression in three dogs.
papers.authors: Bradley K, Ross E, Zarin J, Cole S
papers.abstract: Three dogs with advanced myxomatous mitral valve disease underwent left atrial decompression (LAD) via transseptal puncture and balloon atrial septostomy as a palliative treatment for refractory left-sided congestive heart failure. Variable degrees of pulmonary hypertension were present at the time of LAD. Each dog initially exhibited predominantly left-to-right shunting across the iatrogenic atrial septal defect but subsequently developed clinically relevant right-to-left shunting in the postoperative period. Progressive hypoxaemia, haemodynamic instability and clinical deterioration occurred in all cases, culminating in death or euthanasia. Right-to-left shunting following LAD has not been previously reported in dogs. These cases illustrate the potential for adverse shunt reversal in dogs with and emphasize the importance of careful case selection and postprocedural monitoring.

papers.title: Removal of a lodged endotracheal tube in an anaesthetised French Bulldog using manual laryngeal stabilisation and neuromuscular blockade, and subsequent complications.
papers.authors: Benham-Crosswell F, Armour M, Martinez CP, Lee K, Barfield D, Pelligand L
papers.abstract: A 5-year-old, female neutered French Bulldog presented under anaesthesia with an endotracheal tube (ETT) lodged in the larynx. Cuff inflation and deflation, application of lubricant, ETT rotation, and repeated traction did not allow ETT removal. The ETT was successfully removed under neuromuscular blockade with manual laryngeal stabilisation: the left thumb pressed against the epiglottis intraorally and the left index and middle fingers gripped the larynx externally to immobilise the larynx. The right-hand applied traction to the ETT, which could then be extracted. The dog's larynx obstructed on recovery from anaesthesia with suspected temporary laryngeal paralysis. The dog was managed with a tracheostomy tube for 3 days and made a good recovery. The dog presented in respiratory distress 4 weeks later with tracheal stenosis that was successfully treated with tracheal resection and anastomosis. This case report describes the use of neuromuscular blockade and manual laryngeal stabilisation to remove a lodged ETT and reflects on the subsequent complications.

papers.title: Higher early radiographic bone healing scores with popliteus muscle preservation during tibial plateau levelling osteotomy in dogs.
papers.authors: Sassaroli S, Salvaggio A, Roggiolani F, Fordellone M, Ciabocco F, Palumbo Piccionello A
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare early radiographic bone healing 45 days after tibial plateau levelling osteotomy performed with popliteus muscle detachment versus a modified technique preserving the muscle and to determine whether muscle preservation influences post-operative osteotomy stability through measurement of rock-back. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this prospective, blinded, randomised clinical study (2022 to 2025), 100 client-owned dogs with unilateral cranial cruciate ligament rupture were allocated to traditional surgery (n = 50) or popliteus-sparing surgery (n = 50). Radiographic assessment was performed preoperatively, immediately post-operatively and 45 days after surgery. Bone healing was evaluated using two validated radiographic scoring systems. Osteotomy stability was assessed by measuring the change in tibial plateau angle between the immediate post-operative and 45-day radiographs. Multivariable linear regression models were used to adjust for baseline clinical variables. A P-value <.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS: Dogs undergoing popliteus-sparing surgery demonstrated higher bone healing scores at 45 days, with an adjusted mean difference of 1.95 (95% confidence interval 0.91 to 2.99) on the 10-point bone healing scale and 1.87 (95% confidence interval 0.88 to 2.86) on the modified radiographic union scale. There was no clinically relevant difference in post-operative tibial plateau angle change between groups, with an adjusted mean difference of 0.26 degrees (95% confidence interval -0.10 to 0.63). No major intraoperative vascular complications were recorded. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Tibial plateau levelling osteotomy performed without detachment of the popliteus muscle represents a safe and effective alternative to the traditional technique. Popliteus muscle preservation during tibial plateau levelling osteotomy was associated with higher radiographic bone healing scores at 45 days, without evidence of increased osteotomy instability. Whether this radiographic difference translates into improved clinical recovery or limb function remains unknown.

papers.title: Ultrasonographic detection of joint lesions in canine leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania infantum.
papers.authors: Oliveira PV, Muramoto C, da Costa CF, Estrela-Lima A, da Luz TC, Gomes LFF, Soares da Silva AR, de Pinho FA, Barrouin-Melo SM
papers.abstract: Canine leishmaniasis (CanL), caused by Leishmania infantum, is a multisystemic disease with substantial musculoskeletal involvement. We aimed to assess the usefulness of USG in diagnosing joint abnormalities in dogs with CanL using a clinical approach. Forty-three L. infantum PCR-positive dogs underwent comparative orthopedic physical examination and joint USG; 20 (20/43) also underwent radiography. Tarsal joints were systematically imaged, whereas other joints were imaged if they showed orthopedic clinical signs. Tarsal lesions were detected by joint USG in 86% (37/43) of the dogs, with osteophytes (83.8%), joint effusion (64.9%), and capsular thickening (59.4%) being the most frequent. Radiography detected tarsal lesions in 40% (8/20) of the dogs. As a definitive gold-standard procedure was not available, physical orthopedic examination served as the reference to assess method sensitivity for detecting joint alterations; USG demonstrated 89.7% sensitivity, whereas radiography demonstrated 46.7%. Overall, 86% (37/43) of the dogs had ultrasonographic joint alterations consistent with degenerative processes associated with chronic inflammation. In selected cases, synovial fluid cytology revealed Leishmania amastigotes, and histopathologic findings confirmed the severe inflammatory nature of the lesions, demonstrating synovial membrane thickening and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates. Among dogs with joint lesions detected by USG, 29.7% (11/37) had no clinical orthopedic signs, underscoring USG's potential to detect subclinical joint involvement. Using this hitherto inedited approach, we conclude that USG outperformed radiography in detecting arthropathy in CanL, including cases without overt clinical signs of joint alteration. This supports recommending joint USG as a first-line procedure for the early diagnosis of arthropathy in dogs with L. infantum infection.

papers.title: Urothelial Carcinoma in a Cat with Bilateral Ectopic Ureters.
papers.authors: Piazza C, Seidel E, Dhumeaux M, Vallefuoco R, Fina C, Ronaldson H, Alloway E, Dye C
papers.abstract: A 10-year-old neutered female Maine Coon was presented with haematuria, weight loss, polyuria/polydipsia and progressive azotaemia. Diagnostic imaging revealed bilateral renal pelvic dilation, ureteral distension and ectopic ureters. Bacterial pyelonephritis was diagnosed, but the azotaemia progressed despite antibiotic therapy, and suspected ureteral obstruction prompted surgical ureteral reimplantation. The visualisation of omental nodules and thickening of the ectopic right ureterovesicular junction intraoperatively raised suspicion of malignancy, and histopathology revealed urothelial carcinoma with carcinomatosis. The cat was euthanised postoperatively due to clinical deterioration, characterised by persistent oliguria and progressive azotemia. Clinicians should consider malignancy as a differential in cats with ectopic ureters and an atypical or refractory clinical course.

papers.title: Trial of erythropoietin and platelet rich plasma as adjunctive treatment in dogs with paraplegia and absent pain perception after thoracolumbar intervertebral disc extrusion and surgical decompression: A clinical pilot study.
papers.authors: Janzen M, Faissler D, Rozanski E, Kowaleski MP
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To assess the effectiveness of adjunctive treatment with either systemic erythropoietin or local platelet rich plasma administered at the time of decompressive surgery in dogs with severe spinal cord injury (SCI). STUDY DESIGN: Prospective randomized study. ANIMALS: A total of 32 client owned dogs presented for acute onset of paraplegia and loss of pain perception after a thoracolumbar disc extrusion. METHODS: All dogs underwent a standard laminectomy within 24 h after admission and were randomly assigned to one of the following treatment groups: (1) Subarachnoid saline (controls), (2) subarachnoid autologous platelet rich plasma (PRP), or (3) subarachnoid saline plus IV erythropoietin (EPO). Examinations were performed initially at the time of admission, and 1, 3, 7-, 14-, 42-, and 84-days post-surgery. Parameters of interest included return of pain perception, motor or ambulatory function, and fecal or urinary continence. Statistical analysis was performed with SPSS for Windows 30 software with p < .05. RESULTS: The median age of the 32 dogs enrolled was 5 years (3-12.5 years). Dachshunds were the most common breed. One dog (3.1%) developed myelomalacia 4 days post-surgery and was euthanized. Three months post-surgery, 24/32 (75%) dogs regained ambulatory function whereas 7/32 (21.8%) did not. There was no overall difference among groups. Dogs treated with EPO appeared to have a trend towards a reduction in incontinence (Fisher exact test, p = .089) but a larger study is needed to verify this apparent finding. CONCLUSION: The use of EPO might be beneficial to reduce the likelihood of incontinence, but the low number of patients prohibits definitive conclusions. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: There was no statistically significant clinical benefit found associated with local application of PRP and systemic injection of EPO at the time of decompressive surgery.

papers.title: Complete surgical excision of a type V-variant dermoid sinus (V/VI overlap) associated with spina bifida in a Shiba Inu dog: A case report.
papers.authors: Jeong JE, Kim SY, Kim JI
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe the clinical, imaging, surgical, and histopathologic features of a type V/VI overlap dermoid sinus (DS), and highlight diagnostic and therapeutic considerations. STUDY DESIGN: Case report. ANIMAL: A 16-month-old spayed female Shiba Inu dog. METHODS: The Shiba Inu initially presented at 4 months of age with a dorsal thoracic hair tuft. Radiography and ultrasonography suggested a DS; contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were declined. The dog presented 12 months later for malodor, erythema, pruritus, focal pain on palpation, intermittent discomfort, and decreased appetite, although neurologic status remained normal. CT and MRI revealed spina bifida at T12 and a sinus tract extending from the skin to the dorsal dura mater, with mild dorsal displacement of the dura. Surgical excision via dorsal laminectomy and partial durectomy allowed en bloc removal of the tract and fibrous dural attachment. RESULTS: Histopathology confirmed a keratin-filled dermoid cyst lined by adnexal epithelium with pyogranulomatous inflammation and a fibrous dural connection, consistent with a type V/VI overlap DS. Recovery was uneventful, with no recurrence or neurologic deficits at the 12-month follow-up. CONCLUSION: Dural attachment may lead to clinical discomfort, even if neurological deficits are not present. Intraoperative assessment, histopathology, and advanced diagnostic imaging modalities such as CT and MRI are essential for surgical planning and accurate classification. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE/IMPACT: This is the first report of a Shiba Inu with a type V/VI overlap DS and thoracic spina bifida. Early surgical intervention based on an integrated approach can lead to a good long term patient outcome.
